Shop owners, sorry, it wasn’t a snub! Well, unless you suck. Or are a chain. If not, email me.

title: The Best Restaurants Near Columbia University - New York - The Infatuation
author: Willa Moore; Sonal Shah; Neha Talreja; Will Hartman
text:
#### Willa Moore

Staff Writer, NYC

Willa was raised in Brooklyn and now lives in Brooklyn, which means her favorite bagel place hasn't changed since birth.

NYCGuide

photo credit: Alex Staniloff

Known to Columbia students as the university's version of a college town, Morningside Heights is basically just a fancy way of referring to the area between 110th and 125th streets, west of Morningside Park. Whether you're a student, visiting a student, attending a conference in the area, or just lost on your way to __Harlem__ or the __Upper West Side__, there are some pretty good places to eat around the area. For fueling up between study sessions, family meals, or important first dates, add these 17 spots to your rotation.

Unrated: Restaurants we want to re-visit before assigning a rating. We only rate spots where you can eat a full meal. We won’t rate a coffee shop, bar that only serves peanuts, or dessert shop.

The best bagels in NYC are just south of the neighborhood at 108th St., with a long line every weekend to prove it. The only thing that’s changed about this place since it opened is that in April 2024, that very long line full of Columbia students and neighborhood regulars __changed direction__. (Monumental.) The bagels are small and round, with a springy, doughy inside and a blistered bottom. Bring cash, get an everything bagel—untoasted—with scallion cream cheese, and then take it to Riverside Park.

Alex Staniloff

If you're willing to trek all the way down to 105th Street, you can get your hands on some of the best pizza our city has to offer. Mama’s Too serves textbook-perfect New York slices, but you should prioritize the thicker square slice here. Always get the pepperoni, with its soft, greasy mozzarella and extra-crispy edges, but don’t shy away from the more creative combinations too: the poached pear with gorgonzola and hot honey works shockingly well, and the creamy cacio e pepe is as overwhelming as it is delicious. They also make big, saucy sandwiches on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Mama’s Too is a block and a half from Riverside Park, so bring your haul there for a picnic—none of the slices or sandwiches should be eaten standing up.

Emily Schindler

One of the reasons we love Bánh so much is because it’s equally as great on a cold winter night as it is on a summer afternoon. Picking up a pre-Central Park-walk bánh mi? Flawless. Trying to get a walk-in table in February for a third date that involves sharing a bowl of phở? Also a stellar move. But what’s really great here are the other snacks and sandwiches, especially the bánh chưng chiên, a crunchy glob of fried glutinous rice full of savory pork and mung beans.

David A. Lee

The people behind the counter at Saiguette wear headsets—right away, you can tell that this little Vietnamese takeout-only spot is a very serious operation. They have everything from phở and nem to grilled flank steak over rice, but the real reason to come here is for the best (and largest) bánh mì in the area. Our favorite is the pork shoulder, but they also do them with steak, chicken, and shrimp. Saiguette is a block from Central Park, so if the weather’s nice, bring your sandwich there.

Noah Devereaux

This family-owned cafe near the 125th Street subway stop is an offshoot of a Ethiopian/Eritrean neighborhood staple Massawa, and it’s a pleasant place, with a front patio where you can hang out with coffee and some work before moving on to a glass of affordable South African wine and a cheesy tibs quesadilla. The snacky portion of the menu also has things like berbere wings and fries, and for a more substantial meal you can get a plate of soft injera covered with a steaming assortment of meat and lentil dishes. During weekday lunch, platters are available for under $20.

Sonal Shah

Thai Market fuels Columbia students in the same way that Red Bull fuels late nights. The market-themed dining room stays packed with twenty-somethings and a steady stream of people picking up takeout noodles and curry. Their selection of smaller snacks inspired by street food in Bangkok are what you should focus on, though. Try the daikon cakes sauteed in a sticky soy sauce, or the Thai Market egg crepe filled with shrimp, hot peppers, tofu, and sweet coconut sauce. Everything is just greasy enough to satisfy you after a long day of running around campus.

At Roti Roll, a Columbia student favorite for over 20 years, you'll find roti, slick with green chutney, filled with onion and tomato, and your choice of protein: try the tender, slightly spicy lamb, and the creamy palak paneer. The rolls have the heft of tamales and range from $4 (egg) to $8 (lamb). This closet-sized takeout spot is open until at least 2am every night (4am on weekends), so swing by for a satisfying snack, or after a night out, when everything else closed hours ago.

Alex Staniloff

If you’re looking for sushi around Columbia that’s not a salmon avocado roll from H Mart—which, let’s be clear, is great in a pinch—check out Sushi W. The __sub-$100 omakase spot__ on Broadway offers a basic option (12 nigiri and two handrolls for $53), and a premium option (15 nigiri and two handrolls for $68), and the room is usually full of neighborhood couples who can’t bother to cook tonight, and a few Columbia students who know exactly where to go when their parents come to town. Each seating is only an hour long, so you can’t spend too much time chatting, but for an efficient, sit-down sushi meal, this is a solid option.

Emily Schindler

For a satisfying vegetarian meal that'll cost you $10 flat, head to Doaba Deli. At this counter-service Indian spot, you’ll get a small cardboard tray with your choice of four dishes—try the dal makhani or the palak paneer—plus rice or naan. You can get it to go, or sit in the all-green room and have a quick meal. If you can spare $2 more, get a flaky paratha, if only to test out the sign posted on the door that says, “Paratha Capital of New York City.”

Alex Staniloff

There’s more to this classic diner than its feature in *Seinfeld*, even though the walls are covered with Kramer cutouts and other memorabilia. Since the ’40s, it’s been a quiet corner retreat for students and neighborhood folks, with high-backed red vinyl booths and $7 mimosas (or house wine). The affordable diner food usually hits the spot, and there are often just-exciting-enough weekly specials like roast leg of lamb. It’s a perfect place to sit at the counter with a book, get distracted by *SVU* on the TV, and drink endless coffee refills.

Sonal Shah

This pizzeria opposite St. John the Divine opened in 1945, and generations of hungry students, often with their parents, have granted it eternal life—we hope. It’s pure old-school Italian, with red-checked tablecloths, a faux-stone facade, and hefty free bread that sets you up for a carafe of affordable wine and the hearty meal to follow. Come here for blanket-like pastas and pizza with thick gobs of cheese, à la Domino’s.

Sonal Shah

With a full bar and a porch-like outdoor area, this Italian spot near the 125th Street subway station is roomy enough to bring your entire extended family, though you might have to strain your voices over the generic remixes. 314 is also a good spot for a brunch or dinner date with sweet-but-strong cocktails with silly names (like Gym Tonico), and a red, white, or vodka pie with a light crust that’s just a little wetter in the middle than a typical NYC pizza. The menu is fully fleshed out with things like radicchio salad, and arancini that come out hot and gooey with a side of marinara that’s more like liquid tomato lava.

Sonal Shah

The chicken caesar wrap at the Upper East Side location of this Italian sandwich shop is the one that went viral, but this location on the west side makes theirs far saucier. (If you're into that sort of thing. You should be.) But if you're more into something with bread, they have over 100 options to choose from—try the Triple “S” Chicken Parm which comes with vodka sauce, or the Brutus with soppressata, mortadella, and prosciutto. They also sell an impressive variety of Lindt truffles. We counted 20 different kinds on our last visit.

Noah Devereaux

You’ve been hitting the books, hard, all day long, and now it’s 8:30pm and you realize you have absolutely nothing for dinner, and a long night of studying ahead of you. You could end up spending way too much on delivery, or you could walk down to 107th and Amsterdam and get a torta from Panchos Antojitos. The cheese is creamy and gooey, the bread is crusty, and it’ll run you $10. If you’re a bit hungrier, grab a burrito, stuffed with rice, beans, and your choice of meat. The tortilla is the star here—it’s chewy, flaky, and crunchy from where it hit the griddle.

Will Hartman

Ban Ban Shop serves fusion-y food across the street from Columbia's campus, so it's a good option for a casual, under-$15 lunch. Try the satisfying sandwich with tender five-spice roasted pork, or the shrimp maki rolls that are large enough that they taste like an excellent deal. This is the type of place you can linger in for a while—the last time we were here there was a college-aged couple who had clearly finished their Vietnamese iced coffee a long, long time ago.

Alex Staniloff

Filled with lots of Europeans and students who prefer to work in a cramped cafe with no wifi, Hungarian will make you want to smoke a cigarette while you eat your cherry danish or apricot hamentash, and sip on some hot apple cider or your seventh black coffee refill. If anyone asks, tell them you're working on a novel.

Noah Devereaux

You know that feeling after a night out, when you think to yourself, "Damn, I wish I could eat a slice of pizza that's bigger than my face”? The $6 jumbo slices at Koronet are actually that huge. They have standard-sized ones too, but the only thing that makes the pizza here stand out is its sheer size, so order accordingly. Just don't get toppings—it weighs the tip down too much.

Noah Devereaux

Our favorite Upper West Side restaurants for all sorts of dining situations.

A few soul food institutions, a Middle Eastern spot with Wednesday night karaoke, and the rest of our favorite places to eat in Harlem.

Inspired by the cuisines and communities of New York City, Tatiana makes fine dining feel fun again.

Staff Writer, NYC

Willa was raised in Brooklyn and now lives in Brooklyn, which means her favorite bagel place hasn't changed since birth.

NYC Editor

A journalist since 2005, Sonal spent many years in India before returning to New York. She still prefers kebabs to hot dogs.

Former Staff Writer, NYC

Neha is originally from California. Now living in Brooklyn, she continues to work on her bias against the city’s Mexican food.

Staff Writer, NYC

Will is passionate about bagels and being disappointed by The Mets. He has been writing for The Infatuation since 2023.

title: 10 Best Places to Study in 14 Best Study Cafes In Seattle With Strong Wifi Stop Wandering And Actually Get Work Done — Libraries, Cafés & Late-Night Options (2026) - Study Nearby
author: SethAmazon
text:
Finding reliable Study cafés in Seattle with strong WiFi is a high-stakes gamble. You trek through the drizzle to a “laptop-friendly” café in Capitol Hill only to find that “friendly” means three shared outlets for fifty people and a WiFi password that expires every thirty minutes. Most spots close at 6:00 PM just as your second wind kicks in, and the ones that stay open are often so loud you might as well be studying inside a construction site.

The struggle is real: the “Seattle Freeze” applies to available seating just as much as it does to the locals. We’ve all done the awkward lap around a shop, laptop bag hitting chairs, looking for that one mythical table near a power source. This guide is built for the students, developers, and remote workers who are tired of the “no-laptop” weekend policies and the $7 lattes that don’t even buy you a stable connection.

Whether you need a library-quiet zone in the U-District or a high-energy roastery in Belltown, we’ve vetted these other study spots in Seattle to ensure they actually serve your productivity. If you’re looking for study spots across Washington more broadly, you’ll find that Seattle has the highest concentration of high-speed hubs, provided you know where the hidden outlets are.

## 1. Brown Study Coffee Place

**Address:** 2212 NE 65th St, Seattle, WA 98115

**Best for:** Deep, uninterrupted focus and library-level silence.

Brown Study is the gold standard for North Seattle productivity. Unlike most cafes that try to be a “third place” for socializing, this spot is built specifically for work, with a layout that prioritizes individual desks and a culture of silence that makes a library feel rowdy. The aesthetic is minimalist and clean, perfect for clearing your head before a big deadline.

The infrastructure here is unmatched: the WiFi is enterprise-grade and capable of handling heavy video rendering or code deployments. Outlets are integrated into almost every seating station, so you never have to hunt for power. The noise level is strictly “whisper-only,” which is enforced by the general vibe of the patrons.

It’s located near the Roosevelt/U-District border, easily accessible via the Link Light Rail. It fills up fast with graduate students, so arriving before 10:00 AM is a necessity if you want the best desk.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Mon–Fri 7:00 AM – 7:00 PM; Sat–Sun 8:00 AM – 6:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**A 10-minute walk from Roosevelt Link Station; Route 62 stops nearby. Free street parking in the surrounding residential blocks.
- 
**Amenities:**Fiber WiFi, outlets at every seat, ergonomic chairs, tea and espresso.
- 
**Nearby features:**Whole Foods, Ravenna Park for a brain break.

**Downside:** It is *too* quiet for anyone needing to take a quick Zoom call or collaborate; the “no-talking” vibe is intense.

## 2. Ada’s Technical Books and Café

**Address:** 425 15th Ave E, Seattle, WA 98112

**Best for:** Creative inspiration and technical deep-dives.

Ada’s is a Capitol Hill institution that doubles as a bookstore for the intellectually curious. The tables are literally made of old science manuals and glass-encased technical parts, creating an atmosphere that feels like a laboratory for ideas. It’s small, intimate, and perpetually smells of high-end espresso and old paper.

The WiFi is remarkably stable, even when the shop is at capacity. Seating is a mix of small tables and a slightly larger communal area in the back. Because it’s a bookstore first, the noise level stays at a manageable hum rather than a roar.

Parking on 15th Ave is a nightmare, so plan to walk from the light rail or take the bus. The food menu is vegetarian-heavy and actually good enough to justify staying through lunch.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 8:00 AM – 8:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**Route 10 stops right outside; 12-minute walk from Capitol Hill Link Station. Street parking is strictly metered or 2-hour limited.
- 
**Amenities:**Reliable WiFi, moderate outlet access (check under the perimeter benches), full vegetarian kitchen.
- 
**Nearby features:**Volunteer Park, various 15th Ave eateries.

**Downside:** Weekend “no-laptop” policies are sometimes enforced during peak brunch hours to keep tables turning.

## 3. Zoka Coffee Roaster (University Village)

**Address:** 2901 NE Blakeley St, Seattle, WA 98105

**Best for:** Students needing a high-energy environment with plenty of table space.

If you are a UW student, Zoka is likely already your second home. The University Village location is massive, featuring high ceilings and a wide variety of seating from plush couches to long communal tables. It’s loud, buzzy, and full of the collective energy of people cramming for finals.

The WiFi is generally strong, though it can lag during peak mid-term seasons when 100+ devices are connected. Outlets are plentiful along the back walls and under the long wooden tables. It’s one of the few places where you won’t feel guilty for camping out for four hours with a single cup of coffee.

Parking is free but chaotic because of the U-Village shopping crowd. If you can, take the Burke-Gilman trail or a local bus to avoid the parking lot rage.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 6:00 AM – 8:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**Routes 31, 32, and 75; Massive free parking lot (U-Village).
- 
**Amenities:**Fast WiFi, abundant outlets, high-capacity seating, outdoor patio.
- 
**Nearby features:**Amazon Fresh, various U-Village retail, Burke-Gilman Trail.

**Downside:** The noise level is high; noise-canceling headphones are a mandatory requirement here.

## 4. Seattle Public Library – Central Branch (Level 10)

**Address:** 1000 4th Ave, Seattle, WA 98104

**Best for:** Zero-cost studying with a world-class view.

The Central Library is an architectural marvel, but for students, the real draw is the “Reading Room” on the 10th floor. It’s a massive, sun-drenched space with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking Elliott Bay. It’s free, it’s quiet, and it’s one of the few places in the city where you aren’t pressured to buy anything.

The “Mixing Chamber” on Level 5 is better for tech-heavy work with its computer labs, but Level 10 is where you go for serious, distraction-free reading or writing. The WiFi is public and free, though you’ll need to reconnect every few hours.

Access is easy via any downtown transit tunnel bus or the Link Light Rail. However, be aware that the library is a public resource, and you will share the space with a very diverse urban population.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Mon–Thu 10:00 AM – 8:00 PM; Fri–Sat 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM; Sun 12:00 PM – 6:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**University Street or Pioneer Square Link Stations; virtually every downtown bus. Parking in the garage is $7+ and fills up.
- 
**Amenities:**Free public WiFi, specialized research desks, quiet zones, restrooms on every floor.
- 
**Nearby features:**5th Ave Theater, various downtown food courts.

**Downside:** Security presence is heavy, and the public nature of the building means occasional disruptions or hygiene issues in common areas.

## 5. Uptown Espresso (Belltown)

**Address:** 2504 4th Ave, Seattle, WA 98121

**Best for:** After-hours work in a spacious, classic setting.

Uptown Espresso is famous for its “velvet foam,” but remote workers know it for its expansive square footage. The Belltown location is one of the larger non-library spots in the city. It has a slightly faded, “old Seattle” charm with heavy wooden furniture and plenty of room to spread out blueprints or multiple monitors.

WiFi is reliable and free with a purchase. Because the space is so large, you can usually find a corner that is relatively quiet even when the shop is busy. The outlet situation is decent along the walls, but the center tables are a power desert.

Belltown parking is expensive and competitive. If you’re coming from downtown, it’s a quick walk or a 2-minute bus ride.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 6:00 AM – 7:00 PM (Hours vary by season)
- 
**Transit/Parking:**Routes 1, 2, 3, 4, 13; Street parking is metered and expensive.
- 
**Amenities:**Strong WiFi, large tables, diverse seating, decent food menu.
- 
**Nearby features:**Seattle Center, various Belltown bars for a post-work drink.

**Downside:** The interior can feel a bit dark and dated; not the place if you need bright, modern lighting to stay awake.

## 6. Armistice Coffee (Roosevelt)

**Address:** 6714 Roosevelt Way NE, Seattle, WA 98115

**Best for:** Sleek, modern vibes and late-afternoon transitions.

Armistice is the cool, younger sibling of the Roosevelt coffee scene. It features a very modern, industrial-chic interior with plenty of natural light. It’s a great “transition” spot—meaning it’s excellent for finishing up work in the late afternoon before meeting friends nearby.

The WiFi speed is excellent, easily handling video calls. The seating is a mix of high-top bars and small tables. While it’s not as “library-quiet” as Brown Study down the street, it’s much more focused than a typical Starbucks.

The proximity to the Roosevelt Light Rail station makes this one of the most accessible spots for commuters coming from Northgate or Capitol Hill.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 7:00 AM – 6:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**2-minute walk from Roosevelt Link Station. Some street parking, but mostly 2-hour zones.
- 
**Amenities:**Fast WiFi, moderate outlets, outdoor seating, great roasting on-site.
- 
**Nearby features:**Whole Foods, Roosevelt High School.

**Downside:** Seating is limited and the chairs aren’t designed for 8-hour marathons; you’ll likely want to move after 2-3 hours.

## 7. Hello Em Viet Coffee & Roastery

**Address:** 1227 S Weller St, Seattle, WA 98144

**Best for:** A high-quality caffeine kick and a vibrant cultural atmosphere.

Located in the Little Saigon neighborhood, Hello Em is part of the Friends of Little Saigon Creative space. It is bright, airy, and culturally rich. If you are tired of the sterile “tech-bro” aesthetic of many Seattle cafes, this is your antidote.

The WiFi is fast and reliable. There are long communal tables and bar seating that are perfect for laptops. The egg coffee is legendary and will give you the sugar/caffeine spike needed to power through a difficult project.

Parking is much easier here than in Capitol Hill, with a small dedicated lot and plenty of side-street options. It’s also a short walk from the First Hill Streetcar.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 8:00 AM – 6:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**First Hill Streetcar; Routes 7, 14, 36. Small shared parking lot available.
- 
**Amenities:**Fast WiFi, communal tables, unique Vietnamese snacks, printer access (sometimes).
- 
**Nearby features:**Uwajimaya, various International District landmarks.

**Downside:** The space is shared with a community center, so it can get loud during events or community meetings.

## 8. Jewel Box Café (Northgate)

**Address:** 321 NE Northgate Way, Seattle, WA 98125

**Best for:** Working through a meal and late-night sessions.

Jewel Box is one of the few places in North Seattle that maintains a “cosy” feel while being large enough to accommodate a workforce. The decor is eclectic—think velvet chairs and ornate lighting—which provides a nice break from the IKEA-style minimalism found elsewhere.

They have a full kitchen serving crepes and sandwiches, which means you don’t have to leave when you get hungry. The WiFi is solid, and there are many “hidden” nooks that provide more privacy than a standard open-plan cafe.

It’s right across from the Northgate Station, making it a prime spot for those living further north or commuting via the Link.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 8:00 AM – 10:00 PM (Excellent for late-night work)
- 
**Transit/Parking:**Northgate Link Station; massive Northgate Station parking garage.
- 
**Amenities:**Strong WiFi, full food menu, late hours, outdoor seating.
- 
**Nearby features:**Northgate Station retail, Kraken Community Iceplex.

**Downside:** The “eclectic” seating means some tables are wobbly or at awkward heights for typing.

## 9. Victrola Coffee Roasters (15th Ave)

**Address:** 411 15th Ave E, Seattle, WA 98112

**Best for:** A classic, neighborhood-centric study session.

Victrola on 15th (just down from Ada’s) is a quintessential Capitol Hill work spot. It’s less “themed” than Ada’s but offers a very warm, wooden-interior vibe that feels authentically Seattle. It’s a favorite for writers and grad students who want a low-pretension environment.

WiFi is consistent, and the outlet situation is better than the average boutique roastery. The back area is usually filled with people on laptops, creating a quiet, studious atmosphere.

Parking is typical Capitol Hill (bad), so use the bus routes that run along 15th.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 7:00 AM – 6:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**Route 10; metered street parking.
- 
**Amenities:**Reliable WiFi, good outlet access in the back, high-quality roasting.
- 
**Nearby features:**Coastal Kitchen, Smith, Volunteer Park.

**Downside:** Like many 15th Ave spots, it closes relatively early (6:00 PM), which is useless for night owls.

## 10. Suzzallo Library – Graduate Reading Room (UW)

**Address:** 4000 15th Ave NE, Seattle, WA 98195

**Best for:** Absolute silence and “Harry Potter” vibes.

Even if you aren’t a UW student, you can generally access the Suzzallo Reading Room during public hours. It is arguably the most beautiful room in Washington. The “silent study” rule is strictly enforced by both staff and the sheer weight of the architecture.

WiFi is available for visitors via the “UW NetID” guest portal, though it’s not as fast as the student-only network. Power outlets are built into the long wooden tables, but they are old and can be finicky.

Coming here is an “event.” You come here when you need to write 5,000 words in total silence without the distraction of a steamer wand or indie folk music.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Varies by quarter; generally Mon–Thu 7:30 AM – 8:00 PM (Check UW Libraries for visitor specific times).
- 
**Transit/Parking:**U-District Link Station; very expensive campus parking.
- 
**Amenities:**Guest WiFi, power outlets at tables, restrooms, absolute silence.
- 
**Nearby features:**The Ave (University Way) for cheap eats.

**Downside:** Visitor WiFi can be a pain to set up, and you cannot bring anything other than bottled water into the main reading room.

## 11. Miro Tea (Ballard)

**Address:** 1545 NW Market St, Seattle, WA 98107

**Best for:** A lower-caffeine, high-focus environment.

If coffee makes you jittery and anxious about your deadlines, head to Miro Tea in Ballard. It is a spacious, calm environment with an incredible selection of teas. The atmosphere is generally quieter than coffee shops because you don’t have the constant roar of an espresso machine.

The WiFi is fast and free. The seating includes large tables and some comfy chairs. It’s located in the heart of Ballard, so it’s perfect if you need to run errands or grab dinner immediately after your study session.

Market Street is busy, but there’s usually parking if you’re willing to walk 3–4 blocks into the residential areas.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 9:00 AM – 8:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**Routes 44, 40, and the RapidRide D Line.
- 
**Amenities:**Free WiFi, calm atmosphere, snacks and light meals.
- 
**Nearby features:**Ballard Locks, various NW Market St boutiques.

**Downside:** The tables can be a bit small for those who use multiple books and a laptop simultaneously.

## 12. Cloud City Coffee (Maple Leaf)

**Address:** 8801 Roosevelt Way NE, Seattle, WA 98115

**Best for:** A cozy, neighborhood-vibe morning session.

Cloud City is a community staple in Maple Leaf. It’s bright, colorful, and feels like someone’s very large living room. It’s a great spot if you’re a local and want to avoid the trek downtown or to the U-District.

The WiFi is decent for standard tasks, though maybe not for 4K video editing. There is a dedicated “quiet room” in the back which is a godsend for anyone trying to escape the sound of neighborhood parents and toddlers in the front.

Parking is significantly easier here than in most other neighborhoods on this list.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 7:00 AM – 6:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**Route 67 and 73; plenty of free residential street parking.
- 
**Amenities:**WiFi, quiet back room, $2 “community cup” coffee, kids’ area (avoid the front if you want to work).
- 
**Nearby features:**Maple Leaf Reservoir Park.

**Downside:** The front area is very kid-friendly, which means it can get loud and chaotic on weekend mornings.

## 13. Caffe Vita (Capitol Hill)

**Address:** 1005 E Pike St, Seattle, WA 98122

**Best for:** People-watching and high-energy work.

The flagship Vita location on Pike is a two-story hub of activity. The upstairs loft is the designated “work zone” where you’ll find a dozen laptops open at any given time. It’s gritty, cool, and very “Seattle.”

The WiFi is solid, and if you snag a spot on the railing upstairs, you have a great view of the roastery below. It’s a high-stimulus environment, so it’s better for busywork than for deep reading.

Being in the heart of the Pike/Pine corridor, transit is a breeze, but parking is a literal impossibility.

**Practical details:**

- 
**Hours:**Daily 7:00 AM – 7:00 PM
- 
**Transit/Parking:**Capitol Hill Link Station (5-minute walk); Routes 2, 11, 12, 49.
- 
**Amenities:**Strong WiFi, upstairs loft seating, on-site roasting, heavy-duty espresso.
- 
**Nearby features:**Elliott Bay Books, Neumos.

**Downside:** It gets incredibly loud, and the seating is often tight; expect to be elbow-to-elbow with your neighbor.

## Seattle Study Spot Comparison Table

| Name | Best For | Key Features | Hours | Notable Consideration | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brown Study | Deep Focus | Outlets everywhere, Silence | 7am-7pm (M-F) | Zero-talking policy | 
| Ada’s Tech Books | Creativity | Bookstore, Stable WiFi | 8am-8pm Daily | Weekend laptop bans possible | 
| SPL Central | Free / Views | Level 10 Reading Room | 10am-8pm (M-Th) | Public city environment | 
| Zoka (U-Village) | Table Space | Massive space, Free parking | 6am-8pm Daily | Very high noise levels | 
| Jewel Box | Late Night | Full food, Crepes, Cosy | 8am-10pm Daily | Wobbly/Awkward tables | 

## How to Find Study Cafés in Seattle Strategically

- 
**The “Morning Migration” Rule:**If you are heading to a popular spot like Ada’s or Brown Study, you must arrive before 9:30 AM. By 10:30 AM, you will be reduced to hovering over people’s tables like a productivity vulture. If you miss the window, head to a backup like other study spots in Seattle that have higher turnover.
- 
**The Weekend Laptop Ban Is Real:**Seattle has a growing trend of cafes (like Espresso Vivace or certain Ballard shops) that ban laptops on Saturdays and Sundays. Always check the shop’s Instagram or Yelp before you commute across town only to be told to put your MacBook away.
- 
**Use the Link Light Rail as a Hub:**Don’t limit yourself to your immediate neighborhood. The Link Light Rail connects Northgate, Roosevelt, U-District, and Capitol Hill—all major study hubs—within 15 minutes. It’s often faster than finding parking.
- 
**The “Three-Outlet” Reality:**Most cafes have plenty of WiFi but very few outlets. If you plan to stay more than two hours, look for spots in our list specifically tagged for “Abundant Outlets.” Otherwise, bring a fully charged external battery.
- 
**Etiquette and Purchase Expectation:**In a high-rent city like Seattle, staying for 4 hours on a $3 drip coffee is a quick way to get the side-eye from staff. The general rule is one purchase every 90-120 minutes.
- 
**Safety in Late-Night Spots:**While searching for study spots across Washington, you’ll notice Seattle has fewer 24-hour options lately. If you’re working late in areas like Belltown or the International District, stay aware of your surroundings and park in well-lit garages.
- 
**Check the Academic Calendar:**If you’re heading to the U-District, check the UW Finals schedule. During finals week, every library and cafe within a 3-mile radius of campus will be at 110% capacity.
- 
**Scout with the Complete Directory:**If your first three choices are packed, use StudyNearby’s complete directory to find smaller neighborhood branches that tech-workers usually overlook.

## FAQ

**Where are the quietest places to study in Seattle?** The quietest spots are undoubtedly **Brown Study** in Roosevelt and the **Suzzallo Graduate Reading Room** at UW. Both enforce strict silence. For a more central option, Level 10 of the **Central Library** is generally respected as a quiet zone.

**Are there free study spots in Seattle?** Yes, the **Seattle Public Library** system is your best free resource. The Central Branch is iconic, but neighborhood branches like the Ballard or Capitol Hill libraries also offer free WiFi and desks without the pressure to buy coffee.

**Which Seattle cafes have the most power outlets?** **Brown Study** and **Zoka (U-Village)** are the winners here. Brown Study has power integrated into the desks, and Zoka has long outlet strips under their communal tables. Avoid smaller boutique shops in Capitol Hill if your battery is below 20%.

**Can I find study spots near the Link Light Rail?** Absolutely. Most of the best spots are near stations. **Armistice Coffee** is a 2-minute walk from Roosevelt Station, **Zoka** is near the U-District Station, and **Ada’s** is a short walk from the Capitol Hill Station.

**Are these spots suitable for remote work?** Most are, but be mindful of taking calls. Places like **Brown Study** will not tolerate Zoom meetings. If you need to talk, **Uptown Espresso** or **Zoka** are better choices because the ambient noise will drown out your conversation.

**What is the best late-night study spot in Seattle?** Since most cafes close by 6:00 PM or 7:00 PM, **Jewel Box Café** in Northgate (open until 10:00 PM) is your best bet. Some Starbucks locations are open late, but they lack the vibe and reliable seating of local spots.

title: Off-Campus Study Spots Every Hoya Should Know - Georgetown University
author: Cliff Djajapranata
text:
*Juliette Robinson (SFS’28) is a first year in the School of Foreign Service. She plans to major in international politics and pursue a certificate in international business diplomacy. She conducts research as a Mortara Undergraduate Research Fellow, consults at Georgetown Global Consulting, works for the Center for Social Justice and writes for the Free Speech Project. For fun, she captains the Georgetown Women’s Rugby team and enjoys exploring DC (especially the different food options) with friends.*

Tired of campus and looking for a fresh spot to get work done? Whether you need a quiet library, a cozy café, or a coffee shop with just the right amount of background buzz, DC has plenty of options. Here are some of the best off-campus places to study, write or power through your next assignment.

## Blue Bottle

Need a distraction-free zone? Blue Bottle’s sleek, modern aesthetic is perfect for deep work. Their coffee is top-tier, and the no-frills environment makes it easy to concentrate. There’s usually a steady stream of people coming in and out, but it never feels too loud or overwhelming. Plus, there’s outdoor seating — perfect for enjoying the warmer months. If you like a clean, minimalist workspace with great espresso, this is your spot.

## Compass Coffee

A DC staple, Compass Coffee is all about good coffee and good vibes. It’s spacious, with plenty of seating and a solid mix of students and professionals getting work done. There’s always a bit of background noise, but in a way that feels energizing rather than distracting. Their draft lattes are a must-try, and if you need a change of scenery from campus, this is a reliable go-to.

## Georgetown Neighborhood Library

Want library-level quiet but don’t feel like trekking to Capitol Hill? The Georgetown Neighborhood Library is a perfect middle ground. It’s bright, spacious, and has plenty of seating, making it an ideal spot for a focused work session. The second-floor reading room has gorgeous views of the neighborhood, and if you need a study break, there are plenty of coffee shops nearby. Plus, it’s usually way less crowded than Lau.

## Kogod Courtyard

Tucked inside the Smithsonian American Art Museum and National Portrait Gallery, Kogod Courtyard has to be one of DC’s best-kept study spots. The massive glass ceiling lets in tons of natural light, and the open space has plenty of seating, making it a perfect place to spread out and get work done. It’s quiet but not too quiet: just the right balance of peaceful and lively. Plus, you’re steps away from world-class art, so study breaks are actually inspiring.

## Library of Congress

The Library of Congress is unbeatable if you want to feel like a serious scholar. The Main Reading Room feels like it’s straight out of a movie: high ceilings, grand architecture and a quiet atmosphere that practically forces you to focus. You’ll need a Reader ID card to access the reading rooms, but the process is quick and easy. Once you’re in, it’s a peaceful oasis away from campus. Bonus: You’ll be surrounded by books and history, which makes writing that research paper feel a little more inspiring.

## Maman

Maman feels like studying in a friend’s (very stylish) living room. With rustic decor, comfy seating and delicious baked goods, it’s one of the coziest spots in DC. Their coffee is solid, and their menu is full of comforting treats like chocolate chip cookies and warm quiches. It’s a great place to get some writing done or have a casual study session without the stress of a packed library.

## Tatte Bakery & Cafe

If you like your study sessions with a side of pastries, Tatte is the place to be. With nine locations in DC, every Tatte location is Instagram-level pretty, with bright interiors, communal tables and an inviting atmosphere. The food is great (think Mediterranean-inspired salads, avocado toast and buttery croissants), and the coffee will keep you going for hours. It can get busy, but if you grab a seat early, it’s a great place to settle in with your laptop.

title: Study With the Stars: Find Your Perfect Study Spot at NYU
author: Christian Corpening
text:
##### The TL;DR

- Use this guide to find the best study spot for you based on your star sign!

Are you an NYU student who wants to switch up your study routine with a change of scenery? Looking to establish one but need to find the perfect spot first? Come gaze at the stars with me, and let your star sign guide you toward your perfect study spot on or near campus. Whether you’re an incoming NYU first-year or a soon-to-be NYU alum, there’s inspiration for everyone.


#### Aries

##### Katzell Lounge, Kimmel Center for Student Life

Assertive and enthusiastic Aries is always brimming with ideas and eager to be the source of novelty. More importantly, they’re eager to share these ideas with others. The collaborative, vibrant, yet calm environment of the Katzell Lounge in the Center for Student Life (7th floor) is the perfect place for you to express yourself and stay focused all at once.

#### Taurus

##### Washington Square Park

Taurus’s penchant for seeking out the beauty in all things makes Washington Square Park an ideal study spot for them, especially at the height of Fall and Spring. Let the natural beauty of the park inspire, motivate, and energize you.

#### Gemini

##### University Hall Commons

Gemini prioritizes clear and abundant communication. They interact with the world around them through the power of their words. With enough concentration, Gemini can forge connections between anything. The University Hall Commons is the perfect forum for group collaboration and solo work, whichever one Gemini happens to be in the mood for that day.

#### Cancer

##### 9th Floor Lounge, Kimmel Center for Student Life

Comfort draws out Cancer’s productivity. Of the spots on this list, the Kimmel 9th Floor Lounge provides the most comfort along with gorgeous views of Washington Square Park (you can wave to the Tauruses!).

#### Leo

##### Lower Level 1 Commons, Bobst Library

When it’s time to hunker down for exams, and you need a plan of attack, the Bobst Lower Level 1 Library Commons is the perfect environment for Leo to come up with the strategies that will get them through the season. Many students post up here during exam time for the same reason, and Leo–in their trademark style–stands to benefit from drawing on the studious energy that those around them are giving off.

#### Virgo

##### Vanderbilt Hall Courtyard, NYU Law

Virgo values order above all else. They are able to solve any problem–see clear through any mystery– with their powers of organization and deduction. What better place for Virgo to maximize their productivity than the courtyard of Vanderbilt Hall, the home of NYU Law?

#### Libra

##### North Reading Rooms, Bobst Library

Libra’s greatest strength is their ability to see any issue from all angles and take in different perspectives. Given this, working in groups can sometimes prove challenging for them. The silent North Reading Rooms in Bobst Library (located on floors 4, 6, 8, and 10) would serve Libra best in solo or group work.

#### Scorpio

##### Lower Level 2 Study Area, Bobst Library

Scorpio prefers to move in silence, and you won’t find a quieter space in the entire city than the Bobst Lower Level 2 Study Area. Absolute silence is the policy on the bottom-most floor of the library. Moreover, they prefer to jump head-first into their work and prefer to minimize distractions, making Lower Level 2 the perfect place for them to work.

#### Sagittarius

##### Pier 46 at Hudson River Park

As someone who values freedom, Sagittarius needs a space as expansive as their minds. Pier 46 at Hudson River Park is an ideal spot for them to settle in with gorgeous views of the Hudson River and let their ideas flow.

#### Capricorn

##### Sosnoff Lounge, Stern School of Business

Methodical and high-achieving Capricorn would find themselves right at home in the Sosnoff Lounge in the Stern School of Business. Surrounded by others who excel at strategic thinking and persevering through adversity, they’ll be capable of their best work here.

#### Aquarius

##### Reference Center, Bobst Library

Studying in the Reference Center on the first floor of Bobst Library would be best for Aquarius. As someone whose greatest desire is to bring originality into everything they do, being able to quickly reference just about everything that’s been done before using the materials found in this section of the library would be useful.

#### Pisces

##### Riese Lounge, Tisch School of the Arts

Pisces are the creative tour de force of the zodiac, so it’s only natural that they’d fit right in at the Riese Lounge inside the Tisch School of the Arts. Perfectly content with listening and observing, there is lots of inspiration for Pisces to use in their work.

#### Extra Credit: Use Your Mercury Sign Instead

Many aren’t aware that there is more than one celestial body that influences our identity, our behavior, our sense of self, the way we are perceived, and more. One such body is the planet Mercury, the planet that governs communication, thinking, and intellect. In other words, it’s the perfect guide for picking out a spot for an extra powerful study session. Don’t know what sign your Mercury is in? Check out websites like CHANI and input your date, time, and location of birth to find out in seconds!

Of course, nobody is saying you must to choose the spot that matches your sign. Pick whichever resonates with you the most, and happy studying!

title: Breakup with Bobst with these 5 off-campus study spots
author: Juliana Guarracino; Michael Lando
text:
Tired of scavenging for an open seat at Bobst Library? Disillusioned by the prospect of spending yet another afternoon at the Kimmel Center for University Life? As classes pick up steam, finding a study space that lends itself to productivity is crucial. If you can’t stand the thought of doing yet another problem set or essay response in the Bobst basement, here are five off-campus spots that will make getting your work done sightly less painful.

#### Mulberry Street Library

*10 Jersey St.*

Just over a 10-minute walk from Washington Square Park, Mulberry Street Library is an idyllic off-campus study site. While its rows of bookshelves make for a pretty standard layout, when you look closer, the three-story library boasts a subtle urban edge. Large windows scale the walls of the first floor, inviting in natural light, while the lower levels are enclosed by cozy brick walls adorned with modern art, giving a homey feel to a traditionally academic ambience. Furnished with plenty of comfortable seating and stocked with outlets and tables, Mulberry Street Library has you covered for both light and intensive study sessions.

The crown jewel of the library, the spacious adult reading room, resides on its lowest level. Its solid brick walls are lined with chic bookshelves that house an extensive literature collection. The openness of the space, free of the inevitable clutter and congestion of many other libraries, will keep you focused on that thesis statement you’ve been putting off all week.

#### 787 Coffee Co.

*159 Second Ave. *

If you’re the type of person who needs a snack or beverage while knocking out assignments, look no further than 787 Coffee, located roughly 10 minutes from Washington Square Park. Enjoy delicious pastries — the scones are my personal favorite — while sipping on their signature Coquito Latte and pretending to work.

Although there’s ample seating in the shop itself, 787 Coffee on East 10th offers an attractive alternative. Adjacent to the coffee shop is a vibrant co-working space, equipped with all the essentials: large tables, comfy office chairs, outlets, Wi-Fi, a gender neutral restroom and complementary printer access. Here you can tackle assignments in a focused environment with access to all the same resources that Bobst offers, and more. There are two other 787 Coffee locations close to campus — on 101 Second Ave. and 208 W. 10th St. — though these do not have the attached co-working spaces.

#### Jefferson Market Library

*425 Sixth Ave.*

A Greenwich Village treasure, Jefferson Market Library is one of the city’s premier public spaces. Equipped with all the basics you need to get through an upcoming French project or lab write-up, this library blows Kimmel’s seventh floor out of the water. Originally built as a courthouse in the 1870s, the New York Public Library branch building is an architectural marvel. Unique for its signature clock tower and Victorian Gothic style, Jefferson Market Library is a time capsule to the city’s past and a dream for any history nerd or architecture purist.

The library’s refined stone walls and impressive sculptures make for a grand entrance. To the right is a winding staircase that leads to the library’s palatial reading room. Here, grab a seat at one of the working tables under the room’s high ceilings and towering stained-glass windows. When you need a break between assignments, head down to the lower level modern art gallery. On your way out, visit the attached Jefferson Market Garden, a tranquil site to catch up on emails or review your to-do list for the coming week.

#### Amano Café

*172 W. Fourth St.*

Located in the West Village, Amano Café is a homey coffee shop ideal for any student struggling through their Text & Ideas essay or Calculus II homework. Translating to “by hand” in Spanish, Amano prioritizes freshness from cultivation to cup. The cafe offers a delectable food and drink selection — I love their cappuccino paired with a slice of their banana loaf — great fuel for any study session.

Despite its location in a bustling neighborhood, the cafe still manages to encourage focus and quiet work. It has a cozy seating area with free Wi-Fi and outlets, making it convenient to buckle down and get going on assignments. Although it doesn’t have a restroom for patrons, the shop is thankfully less than a five-minute walk from university buildings.

#### Stuyvesant Square Park

*9 Rutherford Place*

Are you someone who needs fresh air for a solid study session? Try Stuyvesant Square Park in Gramercy. Though it might seem unconventional for a study location, Stuyvesant Square is a peaceful venue for those hoping to escape the clamor of Washington Square Park and NYU. Composed of two parallel parks identical in layout and proportion, the large space is insulated from the surrounding neighborhood by majestic elm trees and lush foliage. Here, you can connect with nature all while completing your assignments — a win-win.

There’s seating throughout the park, but its western portion with benches and tables is best suited for work. Pro tip: bring a Clorox wipe or two to clean the area before getting started. Free Wi-Fi is provided on a limited basis, so the park may be more suitable for hand-written assignments and readings. Regardless of what you work on, you’ll be inspired by Stuyvesant Square’s natural beauty.

So, what are you waiting for? Grab your laptop and notebooks and head off campus to upgrade your study game. Sometimes a change of scenery is all it takes to unlock your most productive self.

*Contact Michael Lando at [email protected].*

title: Local Guide for New Graduate Students
text:
## Created by the Graduate Student Organization (GSO)

Welcome to NYU Steinhardt! As your Graduate Student Organization (GSO), we’re here to help you navigate life as a graduate student in NYC. We know that moving to a new city (or just adjusting to grad school) can be overwhelming, so we put together this guide filled with our best tips and recommendations. Whether you’re looking for affordable eats, the best study spots, or fun ways to explore the city and beyond, we’ve got you covered. We can’t wait to welcome you to campus—see you soon!

### Where to Eat on a Budget

text:
24/7 study spaces for medical students:

At the **Sid and Ruth Lapidus Health Sciences Library**, there are 6 group study rooms (click here to reserve a room), a quiet reading room, and a public area with 30 computers. It is accessible 24/7 with a student ID.

At **Eastbridge Landing** (the former NYU Child Study Center) at 577 First Avenue, the carrels on the 1st floor are currently **unavailable due to construction**. However, small rooms on the second floor and conference rooms are available after regular business hours. Medical Center ID is required to access the building at all times.

At **Greenberg Hall**, apartments 5V-B and 5O have been retro-fitted with study carrels. Conference rooms 6V and 5N are also available from 5pm-8am.

Alumni Hall at Manhattan’s main campus will close temporarily starting October 15, 2020, while the building undergoes a full-scale renovation. The closure includes **Farkas Auditorium, Lecture Halls A and B, and the Student Study Center. **

Wireless access is available in all of these study spaces. Additionally, students can print using the Pharos system to either of the two printers in the Student Study Center or to the one printer in Vilcek Hall.

At **Bellevue Hospital**, NYU Langone students, faculty, and staff have full onsite access to the library space during regular business hours. The Bellevue Medical Library is on the 14th floor of the Hospital building (14N12). Unfortunately, wireless access and printing are not available at this location. 

At the **VA Hospital**, NYU Langone students have access to a special temporary study space on the 2nd floor. NYU ID must be used to access this space.

At **Bobst Library**, NYU Langone students, faculty, and staff have full onsite access and borrowing privileges. The student study spaces on the lower two levels are open 24 hours as long as you have your valid student ID. The rest of Bobst Library has many potential study spaces and a lot of resources and is open 7am - 1am normally. NYU students and faculty should have full access to their wireless network, including all resources. NYU provides shuttle service between NYU Langone Health and the Washington Square campus on Route E. Check the schedules on the following web site:http://www.nyu.edu/public.safety/transportation/routeE.html

Medical students should also be able to use and reserve all graduate student study spaces. For more information on what kinds of study spaces are available in Bobst Library, on what floors they are located, and how to reserve them, please check out their web site.


At the** Bern Dibner Library of Science and Technology** at NYU-Poly in Brooklyn, NYU Langone students, faculty, and staff are welcome to come and use the study spaces. For more information on this space, please look at their web site: http://library.poly.edu/


Check out a map of potential study locations to find the one nearest to you.


View NYU Student Study Space  in a larger map

At **New York Public Library**, all members of the public are welcome to use their spaces during regular business hours. With ample space, wi-fi, and electrical outlets, many medical students have found that the **Stephen A. Schwarzman Building**, the main branch of NYPL on 42nd St and Fifth Ave, is a great place for quiet study. Another nearby public library possibility is the **Science, Industry and Business Library (SIBL)** on 34th St and Madison Ave. For more information on public library locations and hours, please consult their web site: http://www.nypl.org/locations

title: NYU Study Spots: Study in Comfort—and Style
author: Staff Writer
text:
Published October 21, 2024

# NYU Study Spots: Study in Comfort—and Style

#### NYU Abu Dhabi

The open, airy NYU Abu Dhabi Library has a domed ceiling and a suspended mezzanine level. It’s a perfect study spot: it provides ample space to interact with faculty and fellow students as well as quiet areas for concentration and contemplation.

“The reading room upstairs in the library is the perfect place to study,” says Angelina Gerlich, a Social Research and Public Policy major at NYU Abu Dhabi. “If you really need somewhere quiet, there’s no better place to go. Especially during finals week, the intense silence is great motivation to keep going.”

The Marketplace in NYU Abu Dhabi’s Campus Center is a gathering and dining space. It also doubles as a favorite NYU study spot. Students come here to complete assignments or meet with classmates to discuss group projects over a cup of coffee.

#### NYU in New York City

The flagship of NYU’s eight-library system, Bobst Library in New York City is a well-loved NYU study spot. It offers approximately 3,000 seats for student study as well as specialized resources, such as a center for music and media. It also boasts a digital studio and a data services lab equipped with high-performance computers.

“There’s a reason Bobst Library is legendary among NYU students,” says Ben Bonnici, a Theatre major at NYU Tisch. “If the towering bookshelves don’t inspire you, the sheer variety of study environments will. From its whisper-quiet floors to the more lively communal spaces, Bobst is the Swiss Army knife of study spots.”

The Kimmel Center for University Life is located in the heart of the Washington Square campus. It provides numerous spots for study, including music rooms. On the 2nd and 3rd floors, Peet’s Coffee and the Kimmel Marketplace, respectively, have lounge areas with comfortable seating in addition to computer stations and dining facilities. Even more student lounges are located on the 8th and 9th floors.

Additionally, the new Paulson Center for Student Life offers students a variety of study spaces. With nearly 40 percent of the building dedicated to academic resources, you’ll find both quiet drop-in study rooms and larger collaboration rooms for group study. The Paulson Center is also home to The Commons, a spacious hall perfect for gathering with a group.

“I love the quiet study spots at the Paulson Center,” says Anjana Rajesh. She’s a Business and Technology Management major at NYU Tandon. “I also love the Paulson Center’s classrooms for group study spots. My friends and I will reserve a classroom and spend the day finishing work there. It’s extra convenient because Paulson also has a dining hall.”

#### NYU Shanghai

NYU Shanghai’s New Bund Campus opened in the Spring of 2023 and offers students a variety of rooms and spaces to study. From the suspended John E. Sexton Bridge to the spacious Magnolia House, there’s a study spot for you. Meanwhile, the campus’ new, 5,000-square-meter library is equipped with reservable solo and group study rooms, a high performance computer lab, an XR lab, and more.

“I love studying in the West 3rd floor,” says Kaye Richelle Duarte, a Neural Science major at NYU Shanghai. “There’s a quiet room with huge windows that’s very quiet. Plus, you get a really good view of Shanghai.”

If you want to take your studies outdoors, the Campus Courtyard was designed to maximize natural light throughout the year. It serves as a serene gathering place for all: its lush greenery and open layout create an inviting environment for relaxation, study, and reflection.

“My favorite study spot on campus is under the friendship tree in the courtyard,” says Nigel Dai, a Data Science major at NYU Shanghai. “I love sitting there to catch up on readings between classes or enjoying coffee with friends from one of our on-campus cafes.”

title: Ranked: The best Bobst floors for studying
author: Ivanka Sun; Christobelle Rudes
text:
It’s safe to say that most students don’t choose to spend their free time in Bobst Library, unless they’re due for hardcore, locked-in studying. Everyone knows how it usually goes: You walk in determined to be productive for the first time in a while, but end up circling each of the packed floors like a wandering tourist. If you’re lucky, you get some cramped hallway seat that feels like sitting on the steps of Grand Central Terminal at rush hour. To save from unnecessary time spent scavenging for a seat this midterm season, here’s a ranking of every floor in Bobst — ranked from absolute chaos to prime studying environment.

**8. Floors 2 and 3**

Unless you’re willing to sit on the bare ground, these two floors have nothing to offer. The second floor consists only of NYU Special Collections, a staff-only section and classroom spaces. The third is closed for renovations. Lacking both seats and people, these floors aren’t even worth a visit.

**7. Floor 1**

The first floor of Bobst feels like Times Square for NYU students. It’s packed with people going in and out of the library, and it’s as noisy as it could possibly be. People nap, eat, take phone calls and just sit for a quick break in between classes. No one actually gets any work done here. The ones who open their laptops and look like they are studying are lying to themselves — they are procrastinating and too scared to commit to a real floor. Save yourself the wasted time and go literally anywhere else.

**6. Lower Levels 1 and 2**

The lower-level floors are for the people who have sold their souls to Bobst, the ones who have chosen to live underground. They somehow manage to survive without a glimpse of sunlight or a gentle breeze of fresh air. They probably don’t know what day it is, and some might even get their Amazon packages delivered there. Sure, you have access to unlimited printing and snacks from vending machines, but are you ready to give up everything else? Don’t be fooled, these people aren’t just taking studying seriously — they are disintegrating on the inside.

**5. Floor 4**

This floor really loves to disguise itself as a study space, but it’s an illusion. Having spent a good amount of time on the fourth floor, it’s safe to say that this is where you go when all of the productive study spots are full. You can try to get some work done if you sit in one of the side sections, but even that’s not silent enough for true studying. This is where people go to socialize first, study later.

**4. Floor 7**

The Avery Fisher Center for Music and Media is located on this floor, so there isn’t much room for studying. This is where you would go if you need to watch a movie for class — or just want to be surrounded by film majors — but that’s about all you can do here.

**3. Floors 5 and 6**

Students here are actually making a solid attempt at doing their work, but they aren’t quite dedicated enough. You’ll hear the occasional crinkling of a chip bag or the loud pop of a Celsius can. Someone will let out a dramatic sigh as they put aside their laptop and surrender to toxic doomscrolling on TikTok. But compared to some of the other options, there’s some possibility for productivity here.

**2. Floors 10-12**

Floors 10-12 are mostly staff areas, and Floors 11 and 12 even have their own private elevator for elite access. But don’t set them fully aside because the 10th floor has a special gem: the North Reading Room. This is where you can have a quiet, spacious desk all to yourself. If you manage to find a spot, it’s definitely worth it.

**1. Floors 8 and 9**

These two floors are so deathly silent that it’s actually scary. I’m afraid to pass through their hallways and accidentally breathe too loudly. If my shoes are a little too squeaky, I get stares from all directions and it feels like a walk of shame. The eighth floor has a few soundproof study pods, and the ninth has individual sensory rooms — both perfect choices for optimal studying. Everyone here is flourishing in productivity, but the vibes aren’t as spine-chilling as the lower levels. This is where you can secure an area with a cold coffee and finish your whole midterm paper in one sitting. If you truly want to lock in, there are no better floors than these two.

title: Best Places to Study on Campus!
text:
*By Maureen Guilbot*

Being a graduate student means you will spend LOTS of time studying – and with that comes knowing where the go-to spots for studying are!

On TC, a fantastic place to study is the Gottesman Library. Gottesman is the largest educational library in the United States, and (to me) it is also one of the nicest places to hang out with friends or study! Depending on the vibe you’re looking for, you can either go to the second or third floors.

The 2nd floor of the Gottesman Library is a collaborative space, so I often come here to study with friends and chat. If you are like me and you like some sound around you as you work, Gottesman’s 2nd floor is the place for you. My favorite place here is around the round tables by the windows because the table curves around you, so you get your own private space while being with friends. If you want no noise while you study, the 3rd floor is highly recommended. The 3rd floor is a quiet space, so it allows for lots of intensive study time – and as a plus, it is also incredibly scenic!

On Columbia’s main campus, one study spot I absolutely need to recommend is Butler Library. Anywhere in Butler, you will be surrounded by books and beautiful architecture. As you walk directly into the library and head up the stairs you will be in the main section, which is popular among students to study. Another great perk of Butler is that this library is open 24/7. This area gets filled quickly – I’m telling you, it is incredibly beautiful, and students know it!! – so the best time to get a seat is early in the morning or after 5 pm.

Next is Avery Library. This spot has incredible window seats that overlook parts of the main campus, so if you really want to feel that studious fall vibe – this is the best seat in the house. My favorite place to sit here is next to the windows because the table allows four people to sit together, so it is a little more private. As the fall season approaches, this is a really great place to watch all the foliage. Pro tip: If you ever want to feel like the Youtube Lofi Girl, go study here.

And my last spot that I think deserves all the love is the Math Library on the main campus. I really like this spot because it is like a hidden gem. The second floor is where it’s at. You walk into the library and head up the stairs, and there are seats located behind rows of math books that overlook a campus pathway. It is typically quiet in this library, so you can get lots of work done, and I almost always find a seat here.

# Study spots on campus to try this finals season

- Dec 10, 2024
- 4 min read

From the many places to study on both Barnard and Columbia’s campus, these are some of the best places to lock in for finals this fall.

##### Photography by Merielen Espino/The Barnard Bulletin

###### December 10, 2024

Bored of your usual study spots and want a change of scenery? With final exam season fast approaching, here is a list of tried and true places on campus that make for excellent study spots! These five locations come highly recommended by students across all grades.

**Milstein Center Second Floor **

One of Barnard students’ favorite study spots is the second floor of the Milstein Center, which belongs to the Chen Library. The second floor is a very popular place to work, and it is particularly known for its green chairs that face big floor-to-ceiling windows.

“My favorite study spot when I need to really focus is always the second floor of Milstein Center,” says Ursula Vollmer (BC ‘26). “I love the open windows, quiet spaces, and green chairs being positioned looking out.” These windows fill the floor with sunlight, contributing to a positive studying atmosphere.

Along with a sunny environment, this floor is regularly quiet and is filled with many different types of work areas, including comfy chairs, tables of different sizes, desk cubicles, couches, and study rooms! Outlets are also conveniently placed at nearly every corner or desk, which is helpful for the long study sessions before finals.

**The Diana Center Third Floor **

Another quiet study spot, often less crowded than the Milstein Center, is the Diana Center. “I adore the third floor of the Diana Center because of the large windows and natural light. That is definitely my go-to spot,” says Ava Caldwell (BC ‘27).

On the third floor, there is a room filled with desk cubicles that creates a beneficial separation from other students so that you can really focus on your work. Like Milstein, the floor-to-ceiling windows allow for natural lighting and a nice view of Columbia’s campus across the street! Together, these aspects help prevent the feeling of being trapped inside, forming the illusion of being outside without bearing the cold weather. Liz’s Place is also located in this building, so a quick snack or drink is simply a step away!

**Futter Field/Butler Lawn**

When temperatures aren’t as low, students often study outside on both Futter Field and the Butler Lawns. At Barnard, Futter Field is a nice place to study because the lawn is wide, offering a workspace in the sun, which provides some fresh air and a change of scenery from the library.

There are also tables right next to Futter Field, which are conveniently placed outside of Liz’s Place, allowing students to be productive and focused outside at a table with food and/or a drink. “When it’s nice out, I love sitting at the tables outside of Liz’s or on Futter in the sun,” says Elle Berman (BC ‘28). “Getting some vitamin D while doing my work puts me in a better mood. My ideal study atmosphere is in a cafe with ambient noise, and I still can have that atmosphere outside on the field.”


The Butler Lawns are in front of Butler Library, providing a panoramic view of campus. Many students bring blankets and food to work on the lawns and enjoy the sun and the fresh air. “I love laying out a picnic mat on the Butler Lawn when the weather is pleasant and sunny and studying outdoors! Finishing up my assignments in nature while people watching calms me, helps me focus, and kills my procrastination,” shares Nyrah Kapoor (BC ’28).


**Butler Library**

Butler Library is the largest and most popular of Columbia’s 22 libraries due to the building's old academia feel. Butler has six floors and many different rooms, including quiet rooms and talking rooms, so you can always study with your friends (or attempt to) and talk at the same time. This is suitable for group work, such as group projects, so you can talk and collaborate with your peers without disturbing others.

Butler is also the only library on both Barnard and Columbia’s campus that is always open. Out of six floors, its first three are open 24/7, which comes in handy when you have a lot of work, need to do last-minute studying, or complete a procrastinated assignment.

In particular, many students find that this library is the most helpful when it comes to having to concentrate for long periods of time. “When it’s exam season and I have to get an intense study session in, I get a table with my friends in one of the balconies in the Butler reading room on the second floor. It’s a really cozy spot and silent. Everyone’s either very focused or really stressed out, and that helps me concentrate either way,” says Kapoor.

Butler also has a cafe on the first floor called the Blue Java Café, which is convenient to grab a snack or some coffee to keep you awake.

**Avery Library **

With two floors of very different atmospheres, Avery Library is Columbia’s Architectural and Fine Arts Library. The first floor resembles Butler with the classic academia feel and wooden bookshelves. However, this floor has bigger windows than the rooms in Butler, which lets more sunlight seep into the space. The lower level of Avery feels more 70s modern, contrasting with the first floor, which is older. Because this library is much smaller than others on campus, it makes for a more cozy and calm atmosphere.

“In some ways, it kind of feels like a high school library, which feels very nostalgic. It’s very relaxed there, and I prefer Avery to Butler,” notes Marika Giani (CC ‘28). In Avery Hall there is also a cafe, which is always helpful for a necessary pick-me-up during the long hour study days!

This list is composed solely of five study spaces that are commonly loved, but there are so many across campus, and whether you choose these or any other of the 22 libraries and other study spots, good luck staying focused with the upcoming exam season!
