title: Best Coffee Shops in East Village With the Best Vibes
author: Rhaime Kim
text:
*Updated January 26, 2026*

There is no shortage of coffee shops in New York City, but here are the 13 **Best Coffee Shops in the East Village**!

East Village is where all the New York transplants want to live (not to speak for everyone, but I’m including myself in that group). While the West Village can be described as quaint and charming, I like to think of the East Village as its younger, cooler sister. It’s no surprise that all the cool, new coffee shops can be found here. If I lived in the East Village, my favorite activity would definitely be visiting all the different coffee houses.

These East Village coffee shops are offering unique drinks and pastries that are perfect for coffee lovers.

## Best Coffee Shops in East Village

### Sweet Bakery Cafes You’ve Got To Try 💕

#### 1. From Lucie: Flower-Pinned Carrot Cake

The flower-adored carrot cake ($10) is just as tasty as it is *gorgeous*.

Each bite is so smooth and pleasantly gooey. Satisfying. Delightful.

There’s few window bar seats in the cute cafe, and 3 small outside tables in good weather.

Great to catching up with the girlies, picking up for a birthday/housewarming/gift, or as part of a date.

📍229 1st Ave, New York, NY 10003

🕑 Mon-Thu (8am-8pm), Fri-Sat (8am-9pm), Sun (9am-9pm)

#### 2. Librae Bakery: Don’t Miss The Pistachio Croissant

Librae Bakery describes itself as a “Third Culture Bakery influenced by flavors from the Middle East using fermentation techniques from Copenhagen”. That description really holds true when you take a look at their menu. They have interesting items like “Pistachio Cardamom Latte” and “Tahini Chocolate Chip Cookies” that you wouldn’t find in a typical coffee shop.

My friend ordered an **iced vanilla latte** ($6), which she said was delicious. The vanilla syrup made the drink pretty sweet (in a good way). While my friend enjoyed her coffee, what we were really there for was the **Rose Pistachio Croissant **($8.50). Think almond croissant, but elevated with Middle Eastern flavors. The laminated dough is soaked in a sweet rose syrup and filled with a pistachio filling. MMM! If you’re a fan of floral and nutty tastes, this will be a hit. We also tried the **Loomi Babka Bun **($7.75), a bread filled with lemon curd and flecks of black lime sprinkled throughout. I really loved the zestiness and tang that the lemon brought—a unique pastry for sure. 

While Librae has delicious coffee, the pastries are what you need to come here for. The flavor profiles are absolutely unreal!

📍35 Cooper Sq, New York, NY 10003

#### 3. La Cabra: Cardamom Bun, YUM

La Cabra is one of the best coffee spots in the city—and for good reason. With roots from Denmark, La Cabra proves that the Danes really know their coffee! They source and roast their own beans in Copenhagen to ensure that they’re only offering quality coffee.

The interior of the cafe was minimalist and modern. It’s a small space, so be mindful if you’re trying to grab a seat. My friend ordered a medium **Espresso + Milk **($5.5), while I decided to try the **Hot Chocolate **($6.5). She really enjoyed her drink and said that the coffee had notes of chocolate and hazelnut with a fruity aftertaste.I thought the hot chocolate had the right balance of sweetness and bitterness (from the rich cocoa). 

Other than coffee, people visit La Cabra for its famous cardamom bun. The cardamom bun had a light sweetness from the glaze on the outside and a soft, pillowy interior. It was one of the best buns I’ve had…each morning as I’m eating breakfast, I’m thinking about how I’d rather be eating the cardamom bun.

La Cabra has proven that its coffee and pastries are worth waiting in line for; next time, I’ll make sure to grab a canelé to go along with my drink.

📍152 2nd Ave, New York, NY 10003

#### 4. Hani’s Bakery + Café: UGH That Triple Choc Cookie

Omzzzz. The triple chocolate cookie is *so* good. The rim is crunches at the bite, with a majority interior that’s the *multiple-bites-kinda* chewy.

The milk chocolate has slightly candy-like flavor and the flaky sea salt adds a noticable punch.

In addition to fan favorites like the carrot cake and cinnamon roll, Hani’s sports some unusual experiments, like the shakshuka tart. Next time, I’m trying the pistachio halva rice krispies!!!

There’s a fair amount of seating, but even on a weekday afternoon, it was a bit hard to find a spot.

Needless to say, this TikTok-famous bakery is worth the hype!

📍67 Cooper Sq, New York, NY 10003

🕑 Mon-Fri (7:30am-4:30pm), Sat-Sun (8am-5pm)

#### 5. Not As Bitter: Freshly Durian Latte 👅

Traveling in Southeast Asia, I experienced the serious satisfaction of durian desserts.

The Freshly Durian Latte brought me back to those days. The complex, unfolding flavor profiles of durian, the sugar and caffeine rush cooled down my innards on a blistering hot NYC summer day.

The interior is black but the lighting is white and bright. It’s a fun place to hang with friends and is good for working (during the work week, it gets busy during peak hours).

📍241 E 10th St, New York, NY 10003

🕑 Mon-Sun (8am-6pm)

### Best For Working

#### 6. Isshiki Matcha: Minimalist Tea Shop

Amidst the darker cafe-cum-bar vestige of Western coffee shops, I used to dearly miss the clean-cut, light wood adorned Japanese tea shop vibes I’d grown up with in Korea.

In the past 5-10 years, though, these tea shops have been on the rise on both coasts — like Isshiki!

It’s a fantastic place to caffeinate with a matcha or hojicha and crank out some work. There’s a nook of 3 tables with outlets and the wifi is reliable (25 Mbps download, 27 Mbps upload speeds).

Did I mention that choosing alternative milks is free?!!? (I’m lactose intolerant lolol so this is a plus)

📍138 2nd Ave, New York, NY 10003 (it’s inside Moko)

#### 7. 787 Coffee: PR Coffee + Laptop-Friendly

787 Coffee grows, processes, and roasts all their beans from a farm in Puerto Rico—which speaks volumes to their dedication to providing quality coffee. I love how they incorporated Latin American influences and flavors into their menu offerings. Try and tell me that a “Horchata Latte” or “Dulce de Leche Latte” doesn’t sound good.

I decided to order their **classic cold brew **($6.25). The price was quite steep for just a cold brew, but was justified after I tried the coffee and tasted its richness. I’m not the biggest alcohol drinker, so I didn’t get their rum infused espresso; people rave about it and its hint of cinnamon! 

There were quite a few people doing remote work in the shop because of the free wifi, so this is a great place to grab a drink and be productive. They also have other 16 storefronts across NYC like in the Upper East Side or the Financial District! From the sheer amount of locations, there’s no excuse for not being able to go visit one…

📍131 E 7th St, New York, NY 10009

### Best Cafes With Proper Food

#### 8. Smør: Nordic Cafe That Makes NYC Worth It

This Nordic-inspired cafe and eatery is such an incredibly pleasant experience all around.

On good weather days, the high-ceiling grid window lets in so much light into the small but beautifully laid out interior.

Louis Poulsen tiered pendant lights hang above simple natural-wood table booths.

The open-faced smørrebrød sandwiches were plated artfully.

The smoked salmon smørrebrød hit the spot ($10.50). The salmon went beautifully together with the dense rye slice, brought together with dill creme and brightened with lemon curd and pickled onion.

Surprisingly, though, the banana bread stole the show ($11). Each bite was a soft, warm delight. The whipped mascarpone dotted with vanilla made for a satisfyingly heavy finish.

Given the light and 3 table booths, this place makes for a happy place to work. There’s bathrooms but no outlets.

Laptops are allowed Mon-Thu from 11am-4pm, except if it’s unusually busy then. The wifi is fast (136.4 Mbps download, 0.08 Mbps upload).

📍441 E 12th St, New York, NY 10009

🕑 Mon: Closed, Tue-Thu (11am-10pm), Fri (11am-11pm), Sat (10am-11pm), Sun (10am-10pm)

#### 9. Hi-Collar: Japanese Kissaten Cafe In Little Tokyo

Hi-Collar would not be the first place that comes to mind if we’re talking about coffee shops, but it knows how to make some serious coffee. It’s a Japanese kissaten cafe that serves food and coffee during the day, but becomes an izakaya bar at night (I’m sensing a theme here with “coffee by day, bar by night” places in the EV).

They specialize in **siphon coffee** ($8), which is a brewing method that involves using boiling water, vapor pressure, and gravity. We tried their **coffee jelly **($7) that came with whipped cream. It was one of the most potent and concentrated coffee flavors that I’ve had, but it was absolutely delicious. The whipped cream balanced out the bitterness from the coffee jelly and it was such a fun way to consume coffee!

I also had their **Camellia flower tea **($7). It was served in a cute tea set and tasted like a Japanese air freshener, but in the best way. I’m still trying to find out how I could get the tea leaves to make it at home…

This is a perfect spot to get your coffee or tea fix, along with some delicious Japanese dishes (try the omurice)! I’m so intrigued by the izakaya bar, so I’ll have to stop by for their happy hour some time.

📍231 E 9th St, New York, NY 10003

#### 10. MUD: Cozy Late Night Cafe with All-Day Brunch

This cozy brick-walled cafe is the perfect NA post-dinner hangout.

Like my date said, “*they really know what they’re doing here*.” His chai was amazing. As was my tea.

MUD is the brick-and-mortar sister of The Mudtruck, NYC’s first specialty coffee truck. While the Mudtruck is now retired, MUD lives on!

They serve brunch all day and are walk-in only, so get there early on a weekend if you don’t want to wait. Their **all day brunch special** costs $23.95 and comes with any dish and your choice of a tap beer, mimosa, or mud coffee.

📍307 E 9th St, New York, NY 10003

### Best For Coffee Lovers

#### 11. Coffee Project New York: The OG Location

I wrote about Coffee Project New York in my Best Coffee in Chelsea NYC article, but I couldn’t leave them off of this list either! Their East Village location is where everything started, as they now have 5 shops across 3 boroughs.

What’s special about Coffee Project NY is that they place an emphasis on coffee education by offering a Coffee Skills Program at their Long Island City NY location. Coffee enthusiasts, here’s a great way to expand your knowledge of your favorite beverage.

I had their **house drip** ($3.75), which I believe was one of their single-origin coffees.

I also didn’t know this at the time, but their East Village location offers a **deconstructed latte** ($12) for dine-in only. I’ve never seen a latte served in this format—with coffee and milk separated into different glasses. The deconstructed latte tasting flight also comes with a normal latte, sparkling water, and a butter biscuit on the side. Definitely a coffee experience that must be tried at least once!

Coffee Project is one of my favorite places for a cup of coffee, so be sure to stop by any of their locations when you’re in NYC!

📍239 E 5th St, New York, NY 10003

#### 12. Cafe Joah: Korean Cafe With Speakeasy

You don’t have to travel to Korea to experience a Korean cafe! Cafe Joah is a Korean coffee cafe with a speakeasy in the back at night that serves booze-free cocktails and a small selection of bites. There’s not that much seating in the cafe, save for 2 stools and a small bench.

I got the **Iced Latte with Honey **($6), which was an additional $0.50 to get it iced. Their coffee beans are a blend of 100% Specialty Grade Arabica beans that they roast themselves. I loved the robustness of the coffee, especially when paired with the honey syrup.

I’ve heard that they have some of the best matcha lattes—not sure how true that statement is, but I’ll be back to test it out! I also want to try their Jollypong Latte next time, as it’s topped with some a popular Korean puffed-wheat cereal.

So aesthetic and worth a visit (even if just to see the cute tiger logo)!

📍212 Avenue A, New York, NY 10009

### Quick Neighborhood Stops

#### 13. Saltwater Coffee: Tasty Drinks In A Tidy Space

Pick out beans for a pour over or try one of their specialty/seasonal drinks.

The **tumeric latte** ($5.50) was the best I’ve tried — deep, flavorful and spicy. The almond croissant was nutty throughout, tasty even at the end of the day.

The space is tidy and gets sun from the tall-windowed entrance. The wifi is solid and there’s two round tables and front bar seating.

It’s a solid neighborhood spot for to-go coffee, a quick work sesh (no bathrooms/outlets) or to rest for a sec.

📍345 E 12th St, New York, NY 10003

🕑 Mon-Fri (7am-5pm), Sat-Sun (8am-6pm)

## Best Coffee Shops East Village

If you’re trying to figure out what you should do, I have the answer for you. Grab a coffee from one of the **best coffee shops in East Village** and go explore the neighborhood! 

- From Lucie: Flower-Pinned Carrot Cake
- Librae Bakery: Don’t Miss The Pistachio Croissant
- La Cabra: Cardamom Bun, YUM
- Hani’s Bakery + Café: UGH That Triple Choc Cookie
- Not As Bitter: Freshly Durian Latte 👅
- Isshiki Matcha: Minimalist Tea Shop
- 787 Coffee: PR Coffee + Laptop Friendly
- Smør: Nordic Cafe That Makes NYC Worth It
- Hi-Collar: Japanese Kissaten Cafe In Little Tokyo
- MUD: All Day Brunch
- Coffee Project New York: The OG Location
- Cafe Joah: Korean Cafe With Speakeasy
- Saltwater Coffee: Tasty Drinks In A Tidy Space

title: 13 Charming Coffee Shops in The East Village (Local's List)
author: Antonina
text:
Known for incredible restaurants and relaxing vibes, I find the East Village irresistible and visit every chance I get. Finding great coffee shops in the East Village can be tricky, but after years of eating my way through the city, I’ve found the spots worth your time. Over the past five years, I’ve had a chance to try most of the cafes in the neighborhood, here’s a roundup of the best coffee in the East Village for those interested.

This article is a companion piece to our popular guide.15 Iconic East Village Activities (Local’s Bucket List)

**Quick Summary.** Looking for coffee shops in East Village? Here are my top picks. Abraço, Coffee Project New York, MUD SPOT aka MUD, and more.

## Best Coffee in the East Village

## Table of Contents. East Village Coffee Shops

### Table of Contents. East Village Cafes

**Visiting New York City? If you haven’t decided where to stay (yet) check out our helpful guide on **Where to Stay in New York City (The best neighborhoods for first timers +3 to avoid). Short on time? Here’s my favorite hotel in NYC, hands down.

### Abraço

**Website— **Abraço**Address.** 81 E 7th St, New York, NY

Opened in 2007, Abraço is a cozy European-inspired cafe that moonlights as a cocktail bar in the evenings. Using beans roasted in-house, the espresso. Always balanced, the rich shot is the closest you’ll get to Italy without checking bags.

Considering Abraço is an espresso bar first and foremost, you can be sure that any espresso-based drinks will impress, but locals know that’s only half the story. The party doesn’t start without a gander at the pastry case, the olive oil cake is a must-order in my book and pairs perfectly with a cappuccino.

The petite outdoor patio is a hit during the summer months, so invite a friend, pick up a slice of olive oil cake and spend time catching up over proper coffee and really good treats.

**Good to know —** Abraço is one of the few East Village cafes that doesn’t offer alternative milk options, only whole milk on offer. A bit unusual, so it’s worth calling out. 

### Coffee Project New York

**Website— **Coffee Project New York**Address.** 239 E 5th St New York, NY

A quaint cafe with limited seating, I’d bill this as one of the more interesting coffee shops in the East Village because of one clever menu addition. the deconstructed latte. Served as a tasting flight, the deconstructed latte is presented as three drinks. espresso, milk and the final product (latte).

The latte is delicious, to be sure, but it’s the complete experience that makes this such a fun mid-day stop while exploring the neighborhood. Plus, the heavy aroma of perfectly-roasted beans is intoxicating at this charming East Village cafe, I can’t recommend it enough!

### MUD SPOT aka MUD

**Website— **MUD AKA MUD SPOT **Address— **307 E 9th St, New York, NY

MUD is one of the best coffee shops in the East Village if you’re looking to linger for a bit. The service is casual and relaxed, so you won’t feet rushed. There’s a large outdoor garden (heated in winter) great for parking yourself for a few hours while catching up with friends or getting some work done.

As for the coffee? Satisfyingly smooth, every time. I opt for the drip coffee at this location, although the espresso drinks are excellent as well. If you’re feeling peckish, check out the all-day brunch menu for a handful of tantalizing options.

### The Lazy Llama Coffee Bar

**Instagram— **The Lazy Llama Coffee Bar**Address.** 72 E 1st St, New York, NY

As you may have guessed, The Lazy Llama Coffee Bar is a llama-themed East Village cafe. Offering coffee, tea and pastries, the pocket-sized cafe is the perfect spot to re-fuel before getting on with your day. While there isn’t much seating available at this East Village coffee shop, you can head across the street to the small shack in the nearby park.

**Bonus. **While you’re in the area, make sure to check out Russ & Daughters and Katz Deli a few blocks away.

** Local tip. ** Between you and me, the seasonal menu is always better than the regular one. Ask what’s fresh today.

### La Cabra

**Website— **La Cabra**Address.** 152 2nd Ave, New York, NY

Established in 2013, La Cabra offers exceptional pastries and coffee roasted in-house. Originally started in Denmark, the East Village cafe is their first US outpost, a prelude of sorts (they have since opened a location in SoHo as well). Best known for incredible cardamom buns, don’t sleep on the coffee.

La Cabra made a name for itself by specializing in the Nordic approach to coffee, think clean and bright roasts. Fitting, considering the cafe’s motto is “Brighter is Better.” Coffee aside, the Scandinavian decor couldn’t be cozier, lingering is an enjoyable affair (which it why scoring a table is no easy feat).

** Unpopular opinion. ** Controversial take. Ninth Street Espresso makes a better latte than 90% of the Instagram-famous cafes in the city.

### Porto Rico Coffee

**Website— **Porto Rico Importing Co.**Address.** 201 Bleecker St, New York, NY

Charming New York since 1907, stepping into Porto Rico Importing Company is nothing short of intoxicating (the smell!). This tiny East Village coffee shop. From Indonesia to Brazil, expect to find top-notch coffee sold in bulk. Don’t need 5 pounds? That’s fine too, you can order coffee by the cup at checkout.

The decor strikes that sweet spot between cozy and modern, and there’s always good music playing at just the right volume. Don’t overlook the most popular item here. It might not be the flashiest thing on the menu, but it’s consistently excellent.

### Ninth Street Espresso

**Website— **Ninth Street Espresso**Address.** 700 E 9th St, New York & 341 E 10th St, New York

Extracting espresso is an art, the entire process requires great skill and takes years of practice to perfect. Ninth Street Espresso has been honing those skills for 20+ years.

Some argue this East Village coffee roaster deserves credit for introducing New Yorkers to a new wave of coffee and it’s not hard to see why. When it opened in 2001, nobody was offering manual espresso service in the city, and Ninth Street Espresso wanted to shake things up.

After investing in a traditional Italian espresso machine, they set off on a mission to perfect the art of espresso. Thankfully, they delivered. The cafe originally brewed coffee from other roasters before bringing all operations in-house to better control the end product (and we are all better for it).

Seems like locals can’t get enough, the cafe has expanded to three more outposts in the city since 2001.

### Kona Coffee Roasters

**Website— **Kona Coffee Roasters**Address.** 57 2nd Ave, New York, NY

I discovered Kona Coffee Roasters innocently enough. Drawn in by a sign advertising the Waikiki Matcha (pineapple puree, milk, coconut cream, matcha), I knew I had to pop in to escape the heat for a bit. Well, it turned out to be one of the most memorable matcha drinks I’ve had in NYC, I was really impressed by the balanced concoction.

So much so, I returned a few days later with my laptop in tow to get some work done. I started the morning with an. Both drinks were great which makes sense, considering the beans are sourced directly from Hawaii. No wonder Kona Coffee Roasters serves some of the best coffee in the East Village.

### 787 Coffee

**Website— **787 Coffee**Address.** Multiple locations

787 Coffee is one of my favorite coffee shops in the East Village because the coffee is consistently great and the baristas are so friendly. I especially love the cafe’s purpose-driven mission, which is to provide a farm-to-cup coffee experience while supporting the local community.

The coffee is sustainably grown and processed on a farm in Puerto Rico where locals are offered livable wages for the work they do. This the type of business you can feel good supporting, thankfully they also serve some of the best coffee in the East Village! Swing by and see why locals love this spot so much.

### Saltwater Coffee

**Website— **Saltwater Coffee**Address.** 345 E 12th St, New York, NY 10003

Sourcing coffee beans from Sydney, Australia (and roasting them in NYC), this Australian coffee shop serves top-notch espresso drinks (the flat white deserves a shout out).

Since Saltwater Coffee is on the smaller size, it’s a great spot for a grab-and-go when you’re in need of some caffeine but don’t have much time. Luckily, this one of the few coffee shops in the East Village that sells canned cold-brew, so if you like the coffee, make sure to take some home with you!

## East Village Coffee Shops (Post Summary)

Hope you enjoyed by quick roundup of the best coffee in the East Village!

- La Cabra
- MUD Spot

The space itself is beautifully designed without feeling overly precious. You can tell they put thought. I usually order the go-to order and have never been let down. It’s one of those things that tastes like they actually care about getting it right. I’ve watched this place grow from a quiet neighborhood gem to a genuine destination, and they haven’t lost their touch.

# Where to Get the Best Morning Coffee in East Village NYC?

Few neighborhoods match the early-hour charm of East Village. The streets feel calm before the city’s rush sets in, and the scent of freshly pulled espresso drifts from storefronts long before crowds arrive. Finding a great cup of coffee here feels less like a routine and more like tapping into the soul of the neighborhood. Locals value nuance, craft, and sincerity, and baristas across the area respond with a morning experience shaped by skill and intention.

Anyone searching for a breakfast cafe in East Village quickly notices how the neighborhood sets a distinct mood at sunrise. Soft light hits brick buildings, early risers claim sidewalk tables, and the entire area carries a balance of ease and energy. People don’t just grab their first cup and rush away; they settle in, take moments for themselves, and connect with spaces that feel grounded in the culture of the neighborhood. That sense of place shapes the way cafés approach their coffee programs and the way guests respond to them.

The question of where to get the best morning coffee here no longer has a single answer. Instead, it branches into flavor profiles, brewing preferences, atmosphere choices, fresh pastry options, and the personal experiences café owners create for their guests. East Village has built its coffee identity on independence, craft, and individuality. Those themes shine through each morning as more people gravitate toward shops that serve coffee with texture, clarity, and consistent attention to detail.

**The Shifting Morning Character of East Village**

The morning rhythm in East Village has grown stronger over time, shaped by small businesses that value authenticity over sameness. Residents and visitors want spaces that feel intimate, and the cafés in the neighborhood embrace that expectation. Baristas work with an artistry that reflects the neighborhood’s creative spirit, and the experience feels personal whether someone grabs a quick espresso or settles in for an hour of calm.

Fast-paced neighborhoods often lean heavily on efficiency, but East Village balances efficiency with warmth. Cafés open early not only to serve commuters but also to offer a comfortable place for those who use mornings for writing, reading, reflecting, or planning their workday. The result is a morning culture fueled by care and crafted beverages rather than hurried transactions.

The neighborhood’s energy also comes from a diverse mix of people—students, artists, small business owners, remote workers, lifelong locals, and early-morning wanderers. Their different preferences create a rich coffee landscape that encourages cafés to refine their craft continuously. Guests expect bold flavors, smooth mouthfeel, and a level of consistency that honors their time and appreciation.

**What Defines Great Morning Coffee in East Village?**

The local style is not defined by a single roast or brewing method. Instead, it reflects a broader philosophy built on a few essential traits:

**1. Precision in Extraction**

Many baristas in the neighborhood perfect the balance between sweetness, acidity, and bitterness. They treat extraction as a skill requiring daily calibration. Guests notice that attention immediately when they sip a well-pulled espresso without harsh notes or uneven texture.

**2. Beans Chosen with Intent**

Cafés here select beans for personality rather than popularity. Rather than curate large menus, they refine their offerings with purpose, staying mindful of harvest seasons, taste transparency, and ethical sourcing. This philosophy gives morning cups depth without unnecessary complexity.

**3. Emphasis on Craft**

Steaming milk becomes an art, pour-over routines turn into mini performances, and baristas develop muscle memory that produces consistently excellent drinks. Morning regulars often appreciate these small, skill-driven details even more than the drink itself.

**4. A Balanced Atmosphere**

Great coffee becomes even better when the environment supports it. East Village cafés shape their spaces for comfort—soft lighting, uncluttered layouts, and seating arrangements that allow guests to feel at ease, whether they stay ten minutes or two hours.

**5. A Clear Identity**

Some cafés lean toward minimalist décor, others toward homey charm, but each carries an identity that aligns with the neighborhood’s culture. That sense of personality gives guests more than a beverage; it gives them an experience they return to again and again.

**Why Coffee Culture Thrives in This Neighborhood?**

Morning coffee here reflects more than a trend. It grows from unique neighborhood qualities:

- **Walkability**encourages residents to step out early and find their favorite cafés within minutes.
- **A high concentration of independent shops**gives coffee drinkers more meaningful choices.
- **The neighborhood’s creative legacy**fosters environments where baristas and owners feel confident expressing their craft.
- **A strong remote-working community**transforms cafés into essential work hubs where people spend productive mornings with high-quality drinks.
- **Diverse culinary influence**enhances the overall coffee experience through pastries, savory breakfast plates, and global flavors.

These traits together elevate East Village into a morning destination where coffee feels less like a commodity and more like a reflection of local life.

**The Sensory Markers of a Memorable Morning Cup**

Professionals and enthusiasts alike often gauge a café by the sensory details that define the experience. In East Village, several factors consistently stand out:

- Aroma that fills the air before the cup reaches the table 
- Crema with depth, structure, and even color 
- Milk steamed to a velvety texture without foam overload 
- A finish that feels clean rather than muddled 
- Temperature control that protects flavor integrity 

Skill shows up in every sip. Neighborhood cafés rarely depend on dramatic presentation; they allow the coffee itself to communicate quality.

**The Intangible Elements That Set East Village Apart**

Beyond technique and beans, intangible elements contribute heavily to the morning coffee experience:

**Authenticity**

Guests return to East Village cafés because nothing feels forced. Conversations flow naturally, décor carries history, and staff treat guests with genuine warmth rather than corporate scripts.

**Community Roots**

Owners often greet regulars by name. People form relationships with the baristas who start their mornings. That familiarity strengthens the emotional bond between guests and their chosen cafés.

**Creative Energy**

Writers revise manuscripts near sunny windows. Designers sketch ideas at long wooden tables. Musicians brainstorm new lyrics while sipping cappuccinos. This atmosphere shapes the experience in ways no menu description can capture.

**Comfort**

Cafés in East Village operate with a quieter confidence. They don’t rush to adopt passing trends; they support an environment where people can settle in and feel grounded.

**What Morning Coffee Drinkers Look For Here?**

Industry professionals and enthusiasts often emphasize similar expectations when evaluating morning options:

**1. Consistency**

A café earns loyalty when it produces the same balanced cup each visit. Guests depend on reliability, especially during their first meal or drink of the day.

**2. Flavor Definition**

Whether bright, nutty, fruity, bold, or balanced, the flavor should hold clarity. Guests appreciate intentional tasting notes without muddiness or imbalance.

**3. Freshness**

Beans roasted within an appropriate time window and brewed immediately contribute to depth and aroma. East Village cafés excel in maintaining freshness without overextending variety.

**4. Environment That Supports the Morning Mindset**

Some people want a quiet space. Others want vibrant energy. Many cafés cater to both by designing sections that suit different rhythms.

**5. Staff Engagement**

Knowledgeable staff elevates the experience by discussing flavor profiles, brewing methods, and preparation approaches—all without overwhelming guests.

**A Morning Experience Shaped by Neighborhood Culture**

East Village operates with a rare blend of comfort and individuality. Morning coffee here feels rooted in local identity rather than mass influence. The neighborhood values originality, and that value extends to every element of the coffee experience.

Cafés maintain early hours to support commuters, remote workers, and early risers. They prepare pastries fresh, experiment with new roasts, adjust brewing parameters as the weather changes, and refine their approach to both classic favorites and innovative morning drinks.

The neighborhood’s architecture—brick façades, fire escapes, corner storefronts—creates a backdrop that complements its morning charm. Seating by large windows gives guests a view of the slow-building energy outside. The rhythm of delivery trucks, cyclists, and pedestrians becomes part of the experience.

**The Role of Atmosphere in Defining Morning Coffee Quality**

Coffee tastes different when the space around it feels right. East Village cafés excel at creating environments where the drink becomes part of a larger mood. Several atmospheric traits stand out across the neighborhood:

- Soft textures and natural materials 
- Light that changes character throughout the morning 
- A balance of background music and quiet pockets 
- Seating that encourages relaxation rather than rushed turnover 
- An aesthetic that feels curated without stiffness 

These spaces allow guests to enjoy their first cup with intention, setting the tone for the rest of the day.

**Morning Preferences That Shape Local Café Menus**

Many cafés tailor their morning offerings to match local expectations. This results in beverage programs built around:

- Balanced espresso shots 
- Silky cappuccinos 
- Bright, well-executed pour-overs 
- Cold brew with smooth edges instead of harsh acidity 
- Matcha crafted with precision rather than bitterness 
- Seasonal beverages that highlight natural flavors instead of excessive sweetness 

Guests gravitate toward drinks that feel intentional and refined. That expectation guides the way local cafés curate their menus throughout the year.

**Why East Village Keeps Drawing Coffee Lovers Back?**

Morning coffee in the East Village has become a ritual for many who seek a deeper connection to the start of their day. The neighborhood offers more than caffeine—it offers a moment of comfort, creativity, and calm that contrasts with the city’s pace.

The area’s ability to balance craft with personality continues to pull coffee lovers from across the city. That consistency fuels loyalty and encourages new visitors to adopt the neighborhood as their preferred morning stop.

**Why Choose B Cup Cafe?**

Amid the neighborhood’s strong morning scene, **B Cup Cafe** stands out for its warmth, sincerity, and dedication to a welcoming experience. Guests return not simply for the coffee but for the feeling the café creates.

**Reasons guests consistently choose B Cup Cafe:**

- A comforting atmosphere that feels like a natural extension of the neighborhood 
- Coffee crafted with balance and care, produced by staff who take pride in the smallest details 
- A morning environment where guests can unwind, read, work, or connect without pressure 
- Friendly service grounded in genuine neighborhood spirit 
- Consistency that gives guests confidence in their morning routine 

B Cup Cafe highlights the qualities that make East Village shine: character, connection, and thoughtful craft. The café embodies the neighborhood’s essence and gives guests a meaningful place to begin their day.

title: 10 Great Lower East Side Coffee Shops Locals Love
author: Antonina
text:
You might have 99 problems, but finding a good coffee shop in the Lower East Side (LES) isn’t one of them. As a New Yorker who takes Lower East Side coffee shops seriously, I’ve made it my mission to find the very best. The neighborhood is known for being diverse, and the options for exceptional coffee are endless.With one swipe of your subway card. You are steps away from experiencing all the flavors of the world in a single neighborhood.

The Lower East Side is full of colorful cafes that can trace their roots all across the globe. From Korea to Morocco, each cafe brings new and unique flavors for you to enjoy.

If this list helps even one person, then all my caffeine jitters will have been well worth it. 

**Quick Summary.** Looking for lower east side coffee shops locals love in Lower East Side? Here are my top picks. Caffe Vita, Ost Cafe, The Lazy Llama Coffee Bar, and more.

**Visiting New York City?** If you haven’t decided where to stay (yet) check out our helpful guide on ** Where to Stay in New York City (10 Best Neighborhoods +3 to Avoid)**. Don’t have time? Here’s my favorite hotel in NYC, hands down.

## Best Lower East Side Coffee Shops

## Table of Contents. LES Coffee Shops

## Table of Contents. Best Coffee Shops LES

### Caffe Vita

**Website.** Caffe Vita**Address.** 124 Ludlow St, New York, NY 10002

Founded in Seattle in 1995, Caffe Vita has steadily expanded and, lucky for us, opened one of the best coffee shops in the Lower East Side. The secret to their success is truly in the coffee; the company partners with farmers all around the globe to make sure the coffee beans used are of top quality. The beans are then roasted in-house in Seattle before being brewed into your coffee.

You’ll find talented baristas at Caffe Vita making expertly crafted drinks. For those of you who like espresso, I’m convinced this Lower East Side coffee shop has the best in the city. If you see a line out. Plus, since there isn’t much seating (just a small counter at the window), folks are in and out, and the line moves quickly.

### Ost Cafe

**Instagram.** Ost Cafe**Address.** 511 Grand St, New York, NY 10002

Ost Cafe is what my dream New York City apartment would be – bright, full of plants, and charmingly timeless. Despite its small size, Ost Cafe is one of the best coffee shops in the Lower East Side, offering a variety of quality coffee and tasty pastries.

Although there are only a handful of chairs available, it’s not hard to find an open seat where you can cozy up with a book. Manned by friendly baristas, this laid-back LES cafe provides a comfortable environment to linger, making it an ideal spot to rest your legs.

### The Lazy Llama Coffee Bar

**Website.** The Lazy Llama Coffee Bar**Address.** 72 E 1st St, New York, NY 10003

The Lazy Llama is a petite café that offers coffee, tea, and pastries—a perfect pit stop to recharge for the day ahead. True to its name, the LES coffee shop embraces a llama theme, even featuring llama-themed merchandise. Each cup bears an adorable llama logo, making it hard to part with afterward.

Although seating is limited, you can enjoy your drink at First Park across the street, where Llama At The Park, an extension of the café, offers additional coffee options from a small shack.

**Bonus. **While you’re in the area, make sure to check out Russ & Daughters for a bagel and Katz Deli for a pastrami sandwich. The Lower East Side staples are two of the most iconic restaurants in New York City.

** Local tip. ** Here’s something most visitors don’t know. the best time to visit is right when they open. 

### Little Canal

**Website.** Little Canal**Address.** 26 Canal St, New York, NY 10002

Little Canal, a sunny Lower East Side spot at the bustling intersection of Canal, Essex, and Rutgers St., is the quintessential LES cafe. Renowned for its top-notch drinks crafted by quick and friendly baristas, it’s perfect for a speedy to-go coffee.

If time allows, enjoy their mouthwatering breakfast dishes, like the delicious hangover wrap (fried eggs, cheese, bacon, potatoes, chipotle sauce). **Note. Laptops aren’t allowed here,** so if you need to work, consider other coffee shops in the Lower East Side from this list.

### Davelle

**Website.** Davelle**Address.** 102 Suffolk St, New York, NY 10002

Davelle, a tiny coffee shop in the Lower East Side, is a Japanese-style cafe known for its Instagram-worthy toast. Despite its small size, accommodating around ten people inside with a few outdoor tables, the service is quick, and the staff is friendly. Everything at Davelle not only looks good but tastes even better.

With options like savory ham and egg or sweet berry and cream cheese toast, it’s a top-notch LES coffee shop. The menu, adorned with hand-drawn doodles. Alongside their famous toast, Davelle offers a selection of really good Japanese meals and drinks, including the best matcha.

### Black Cat

**Website.** Black Cat LES**Address.** 172 Rivington St, New York, NY 10002

When it comes to studying in Lower East Side coffee shops, Black Cat takes the lead. With free Wi-Fi, a printer, and. While its popularity means constant activity, it’s an excellent spot for group projects or business meetings. If you work up an appetite, there’s a decent-sized breakfast menu to choose from, as well as fresh pastries.

** Unpopular opinion. ** Hot take. you don’t need to spend $7 on a latte to get great coffee in Lower East Side.

### The Grandaddy

**Website.** The Grandaddy**Address.** 290 Grand St, New York, NY 10002

The Grandaddy has spacious communal tables, making it easy to get comfortable. It strikes the perfect balance – quiet enough for focused work but not so silent that you feel isolated, making it my ideal Lower East Side cafe.

What’s more, it’s budget-friendly, with reasonably priced coffee (an americano is less than $4). For a unique twist, try the signature black sesame latte. While it may not be the go-to spot for breakfast due to its pastry-heavy menu, The Grandaddy is an excellent pit stop for a quick recharge.

### Ludlow Coffee Supply

**Website.** Ludlow Coffee Supply**Address.** 176 Ludlow St, New York, NY 10002

Ludlow Coffee Company may seem small and simple, but it’s one of the best coffee shops in the Lower East Side. Despite its minimalist look, the coffee is flavorful. Thanks to a shoutout from Dua Lipa in a Vogue video, the cafe gained popularity. It might have a line sometimes, but it moves fast.

What sets Ludlow Coffee Company apart is its signature lattes—bourbon vanilla, maple, and salted caramel are top picks (my favorite is maple). With plenty of tables and natural light streaming through large windows, it’s a great Lower East Side coffee shop to work in while enjoying your drink.

### Cafe Grumpy

**Website.** Cafe Grumpy**Location.** 13 Essex St, New York, NY 10011 & 115 Delancey St, New York, NY 10002

Established in 2005, Cafe Grumpy ventured into in-house coffee roasting in 2009, propelling their coffee to new heights and capturing the hearts of locals. The company expanded its footprint across NYC to meet the rising demand, establishing two coffee shops in the Lower East Side.

Cafe Grumpy’s distinct logo, featuring a somewhat unenthusiastic (or grumpy) caricature, has become a marketing triumph. The emblematic design on cups and storefronts draws in curious folks to these LES cafes.

What initially may have attracted crowds for a snapshot of the logo keeps them returning for some of the best coffee in the Lower East Side. With two easy-going coffee shops in the area, Cafe Grumpy stands ready to satisfy all your caffeinated cravings.

The Cafe Grumpy on Delancey St. is inside the Essex Market. Enter the market, head downstairs and head towards the neon grumpy logo. The Cafe Grumpy on Essex St. is a standalone cafe.

### Pause Cafe

**Website.** Pause Cafe**Address.** 3 Clinton St, New York, NY 10002

Since opening in 2011, Pause Cafe has been a go-to in the Lower East Side, prompting a recent move to a larger space due to constant lines. Boasting a breakfast menu loaded with healthy options, including delicious super-food bowls, it attracts locals seeking a nutritious start to their day.

Inspired by the owner’s Moroccan roots, the cafe emanates a vibrant North African and Mediterranean atmosphere, with mosaic-tiled bistro tables echoing the colors of its fruity breakfast bowls. Offering halal choices, Pause Cafe stands out as a top LES coffee shop for practicing Muslims.

With such variety, leaving hungry is not an option! Don’t miss the (working) Moroccan fountain embedded into the wall, adorned with small sea-blue tiles and brass accents, during your visit to this Lower East Side cafe.

title: The 19 Best Coffee Shops In NYC - New York - The Infatuation
author: Neha Talreja; Willa Moore; Will Hartman; Sonal Shah
text:
#### Neha Talreja

Former Staff Writer, NYC

Neha is originally from California. Now living in Brooklyn, she continues to work on her bias against the city’s Mexican food.

NYCGuide

photo credit: SEY Coffee

Coffee shops play an important role in our society. Sure, they’re where you go to get your wake-up juice in the morning, but a good coffee shop is also a community hub. Where else would coffee snobs seek out better brewing methods, or literary snobs read Proust in public, or sitcom characters make witty remarks to their five friends? If you’re looking for exceptional brews, or just a good hang, stop by one of these spots. Especially if you’ve become overly acquainted with your robotic office coffee dispenser lately. (For cafes where you can get work done, check out this guide.)

Unrated: Restaurants we want to re-visit before assigning a rating. We only rate spots where you can eat a full meal. We won’t rate a coffee shop, bar that only serves peanuts, or dessert shop.

We once spent around $16 on a pour-over at this tiny coffee counter near Morningside Park, and it was one of the best cups of coffee we’ve ever had—like sipping on the essence of a dozen different berries, all lightly dipped in chocolate. Surrounded by posters of metal bands and the blasting of distorted guitars, the soft-spoken guy who brews these delicate drinks is a devoted metalhead, who named his shop after a __radio receiver__. He uses coffee from Brooklyn roastery Sey, among other specialty coffee brands, and makes his own blends too, but you don’t need to splurge to experience this place—even the regular drip coffee is excellent.

Sonal Shah

Fasan Coffee is so narrow and swallowed by taller gray buildings that you could walk past and totally miss it—if it weren’t painted butter yellow and red. Run by one man whose wife has decorated the interior with random objects thrifted in LA, this tiny Chinatown spot is relentlessly charming inside. The menu has all the classics, like Americanos and lattes, but if you come here and don’t try one of their signature drinks, you’re doing it wrong. For something highly caffeinated, try the espresso cream cold brew, or for something a little funkier, try the yuzu bright brew, which is proof that yuzu and cold brew can be friends.

Willa Moore

On a residential stretch of Crosby Ave. in Pelham Bay, Sundays Off looks like a house, but inside it’s just a small takeout counter. They’re brewing some of the best coffee for miles here, whether that’s a nutty cold brew or a strong turmeric latte. They make some of their own baked goods, too, like bagels, large chocolate chip cookies, and Basque cheesecake, and stock some shelves with gourmet products like maple syrup and tinned fish. It’s too tiny to stay, but you can sit at a table outside if the weather’s good.

Sonal Shah

No fewer than three tools are used to make your espresso at PPL, a tiny spot in Williamsburg that always displays the name of the farm where your beans were grown. This shop started as a clothing brand (which they sell here) and morphed into the kind of place that serves oat milk cortados and ceremonial-grade matcha that’s a big step above your normal iced latte spot. Greenery lines the walls, and the smell of brewing coffee mixed with hoja santa fills the room, but sadly there’s not a ton of seating, so you’ll most likely be taking your order to go.

Alex Staniloff

Interlude is about as minimalist as it gets, with a smattering of tables inside a bright white Tribeca loft. Most people take their orders to go, but if you do get a seat, it’s a peaceful place to recharge with a matcha tonic. The espresso drinks are top-notch, but Interlude’s matcha is near perfect, and not bitter at all. Don’t leave without a pastry—their malted chocolate chip cookie is one of the best cookies in the city—or don’t leave at all. You can sit out front to take in the calm of Hudson Street.

Carina Finn

This coffee shop now has four uptown locations, but the large, plant-filled one in Inwood is great for some espresso-fueled computer work, a catch-up with a friend, or an interaction with a barista who’ll treat you like an instant regular. All of the excellent coffee here comes from small growers in Ethiopia, where the husband-and-wife owners first met. The beans are then roasted in small batches and sold by the pound or ground for use in the shop’s espresso, macchiatos, and cold brew. They have pastries and more substantial food, like injera wraps filled with spicy lentils and vegetables. Buunni also hosts regular events, like community open mics, and many of them are at this location.

Maribel Acosta

This tiny Bed-Stuy coffee shop from alums of Daughter and The Fly is quite the scene on Saturday mornings. People in cow-print pants and emerging clog brands play footsie under the tiny tables, swapping bites of grain bowls and tamarind glazed plantains. The tight, concrete-clad space has a killer coffee program and great snacks, like a breakfast sandwich with soft scrambled eggs, pimento cheese, pickled green tomato, and paprika aioli. In the evening, it turns into a natural wine bar.

Che

Prince might be the perfect coffee shop. The table-service Turkish cafe is a catch-all hub on the corner of Arthur Avenue in the Bronx, and on weekday mornings it fills up with Fordham students and email jobbers. On weekends, the laptop crowd is relegated to a “quiet area” in the basement, and the upstairs has more social energy. Light streams through the tall windows, and groups linger for hours in the expansive space, ordering fluffy coconut Raffaello cake and a succession of Viennese cappuccinos in tiny cups. Outside, there’s a contingent of people who require a fresh cigarette with each cup of coffee.

Emily Schindler

Since opening in Bushwick in 2023, Larry’s has developed a loyal following of people who couldn’t possibly start a Saturday without a cà phê muối. The cold brew with salted cold foam is equal parts salty and sweet, and just as big a hit at their second location in Park Slope. Like at their original outpost, the beverages are the whole point here, such as the Larry’s Ice Green—that’s coconut water with ceremonial matcha foam on top, which sinks slowly until it’s all one lightly caffeinated, highly refreshing combination. But there is a short food menu, with things like lemongrass beef skewers over rice noodles with nước chấm, and tiny Vietnamese coffee brownies wrapped up like presents.

Willa Moore

Sey is something of a rising star in the coffee world. At least according to three separate people who stopped to tell us this during our last visit. Coffee aficionados go out of their way to try this Brooklyn-based roastery’s beans, available at their plant-filled store in East Williamsburg. Sey switches up their espresso, iced, and drip selections every month, and specializes in ultra-light roasts from single-source producers. It’s a nice, airy warehouse with more benches and bars than tables, so don’t count on room for your laptop. Come here when you’re ready to learn what a “washed coffee” is.

SEY Coffee

This East Village kissaten (a Japanese tea room and coffee shop) is one of the few places where you can get siphon coffee. Sit at the bar, surrounded by decorative mismatched china and stained glass lampshades, and your barista will prepare your order as meticulously as any mixologist. Each cup of coffee is made via one of three brewing methods (pour-over, aeropress, or siphon), and they have an exciting bean selection featuring Japanese roasters. You can also get a proper lunch of omurice and various sandos. Just get there before they turn into a bar at night.

Kenny Yang

This Yemeni coffee shop in Williamsburg is open until 11pm on weeknights and 1am on the weekends, but it’s a scene at all hours, especially on the weekends. There’s a small window on weekday afternoons when you can actually get some reading done, but by 4pm, it fills up with friends and families sharing fresh pots of spiced Adeni chai. An evening table in the cramped space can be hard to come by, as people tend to linger over flaky homemade khaliat al nahl, drizzled with honey. But who can blame them—we’re just as reluctant to leave once we get caffeinated and chatty. Qahwah House also has another location in the West Village.

Carlo Mantuano

A beloved espresso kingdom on 7th Street, Abraço has been fueling the lives of East Village dwellers since 2007, with their small cups of biting, chocolate-y espresso, and olive oil cake. That cake is so moist, it could almost be an olive oil brownie in disguise. The pastry and snacking menu here changes every day, but you can always find this treat on the menu. The red lighting and neon sign might remind you of a bar, and you can in fact get cocktails here. One thing to know—they decidedly don’t offer any dairy-free milk alternatives.

Emily Schindler

Remi isn’t the only combination plant shop and cafe in NYC, but it is the only one where you can order a fancy latte and have them make you a matching mini floral arrangement. Naturally, the best drinks at this Midtown spot are floral varieties like rose and lavender, which accent the flavor of the espresso rather than make it taste like someone sprayed perfume in your drink. It’s more low-key than you’d expect for somewhere so photogenic, so feel free to bring your laptop. If you can’t do the digital nomad thing, this is the next best place to take zoom meetings (and make your coworkers jealous). They have another location four blocks up on 48th.

Carina Finn

This stylish Japanese import is positioned right in front of Brooklyn Bridge, with a postcard view beyond its huge arched windows. That’s enough of a draw for tourists and morning joggers, but they also happen to make a perfect cup of coffee. Their signature drink is the Spanish latte made with sweetened condensed milk, but serious coffee nerds come here to geek out over single-origin pour-overs. If you’re heading for a picnic or a walk in Brooklyn Bridge Park, grab a Balthazar pastry to go, or soft serve on summer afternoons.

Alex Staniloff

At Caffe Paradiso, the people behind __Dante__ have swapped perfect Negronis in Greenwich Village for perfect espresso in Nolita. Their signature drinks have some bells and whistles—a foam top here, some shaved chocolate there—that tend to attract people who like taking pictures of their coffee and are willing to stand in line to do so. But nothing on their menu is too sweet or over-the-top. Try the Paradiso Cream Top, an iced americano with thick cream that sinks into the coffee as you sip it. There are a few bar seats, but if you’ve got time, take your drink across the street to Elizabeth Street Garden.

Willa Moore

The pastries are on par with the coffee at this small counter spot in the East Village, and that is very important to us. Aside from expertly made coffee, the speciality here is cardamom buns, and these sticky, airy, delicately-spiced knots of dough are second to none. La Cabra’s pastry prowess isn’t exactly a secret, though, so expect a line that doesn’t let up from open to close. But the line isn’t totally atrocious, and the wait is definitely worth it. There are a few small tables out in front if you want to make everyone in line very jealous.

Emily Schindler

As much as we love our single origin pour-overs, we miss when coffee shops were somewhere you went to see loveable weirdos sing “Smelly Cat.”* *Black Cat LES is one place keeping ’90s-style coffee shop culture alive, in a subterranean space that feels like the common room of a dorm with leather couches, board games, and a piano. On any given night, there’s an open mic, comedy show, or reading, and if you’re a performer, you’ll get a receptive audience. You can order basic coffee drinks, organic teas, and mason jars of wine.

Emily Schindler

Variety is a mini chain, but it’s a likable one. There are eight locations between Brooklyn and Manhattan, and we’re partial to their Park Slope outpost. We don’t know why the coffee tastes better there, but it does. The cafe is big and sunny, with ample seating and fast wifi, and it’s also close to Prospect Park, so you can take a walk if you need to clear your head in the middle of getting work done.

Kate Previte

Is your roommate a pain? Did you forget to pay Spectrum? Sounds like you need a coffee shop with wifi.

It’s easy to find a good bagel in New York. But a great one? You’ll find those in this guide.

A guide to the elevated coffee shops of NYC—the ones that serve great food. Lots of toast ahead.

Former Staff Writer, NYC

Neha is originally from California. Now living in Brooklyn, she continues to work on her bias against the city’s Mexican food.

Staff Writer, NYC

Willa was raised in Brooklyn and now lives in Brooklyn, which means her favorite bagel place hasn't changed since birth.

Staff Writer, NYC

Will is passionate about bagels and being disappointed by The Mets. He has been writing for The Infatuation since 2023.

NYC Editor

A journalist since 2005, Sonal spent many years in India before returning to New York. She still prefers kebabs to hot dogs.

title: 11 Places to Eat in the Lower East Side of Manhattan | That’s What She Had
author: Yulia Dyukova
text:
On my last trip to New York, I stayed in the Lower East Side of Manhattan, less than a five-minute walk from such icons as Katz’s Deli and Russ & Daughters. The neighborhood, while quite loud and hectic, proved to be a great place to explore some of the best foods New York has to offer: from Chinese hand-pulled noodles to third-wave coffee to gluten-free baked goods and beyond. I had two weeks and tried to cover as many places to eat in the Lower East Side as I could.

That being said, this list is, by no means, complete. It is simply a compilation of the places I tried and loved. I hope you enjoy them too!

## 11 Places to Eat in the Lower East Side I Loved

## Good Thanks Cafe

This was an accidental find on my last day in NYC. I had to grab a quick breakfast before catching a taxi to Hoboken and simply crossed the road from my Airbnb to the nearest cafe that looked promising. Little did I know this would be one of the best meals I had in NYC. I ordered toasted sourdough topped with creme fraiche, spanish sardines, and a pistachio gremolata that was absolutely amazing. I loved it so much I later recreated the meal at home.

The cafe itself is quite small and cozy, the service is fast and their coffee is good too. We didn’t make a reservation, but the place was almost full even though it was only 8 am. So it might be a good idea to reserve a table.

## Remedy Diner

While the breakfast at Good Thanks Cafe was my last meal in NYC, the breakfast at Remedy Diner was my first. I hadn’t been in the U.S. for five years and dreamed of having a proper American breakfast at a classic diner upon arrival. Leather booths, coffee from a pot a waitress pours into your cup over and over again, eggs and pancakes, the whole nine yards. And Remedy Diner delivered.

Remedy diner is one of the most iconic places to eat in the Lower East Side. This family-owned business has been in operation since 2007 and is frequented by some A-list celebrities, like Rihanna who was spotted there on multiple occasions (most recently after Met Gala in 2023 with A$AP Rocky). It also served as one of the filming location for Collateral Beauty with Will Smith (if you love visiting famous filming locations, I have this post listing the restaurants in NYC that appeared in films and on TV).

They are open 24/7 and have an extensive menu with all the regular suspects: omelets, pancakes and waffles, burgers. They have a kids menu and a lot of vegetarian options. This is genuinely good diner food, no more no less.

## Boulton&Watt (unfortunately closed)

Boulton&Watt is a great place to eat in the Lower East Side is you are looking for a bit more upscale brunch or dinner. The interior design is a mixture of industrial and vintage styles, with exposed brick walls, wooden beams and red leather bar stools along the counter. They have a covered patio that comes to life at night, when dozens of bare bulbs light up.

The menu is short and sweet which I love. We tried the cheese and chorizo grits with poached eggs and salsa verde which was the ultimate comfort meal without being too heavy. Their burger with bacon and caramelized onions was also great. The place is quite popular for their craft cocktails. I couldn’t try one of the alcoholic ones, but the bartender made me a mocktail on request.

## Katz’s Delicatessen

On to the iconic places to eat in Lower East Side! Katz’s Deli is an absolute must in New York for multiple reasons. First of all, it’s the oldest NYC deli that originated in 1888. Second, they serve the most delicious pastrami sandwiches (the most popular ones in all of New York, for sure). Third, the deli was used as a filming location for When Harry Met Sally (the iconic phrase “I’ll have what she’s having” was coined here).

The one major downside is that there’s always a long line of people outside of the deli waiting for their turn to try the legendary pastrami sandwich, but the line moves quite quickly. You can read more about my experience at Katz’s and a bit about its history here.

**Tip:** there are many amazing guided New York City food tours, including a tour of the LES that will help you cover Katz’s Deli and many other restaurants I recommend in this article.  

## Russ & Daughters

Russ & Daughters is another iconic place to eat in the Lower East Side (if you are after the most iconic meals in NYC, check out this post of mine). The bagel shop — the original location is, in fact, a shop, not a restaurant — was set up in 1914. Over a century later, Russ & Daughters is still considered the best place for traditional New York bagels.

The space is quite small and almost always crowded. As you enter, take a little numbered ticket and wait till it’s called. The line moves fast, so while you are waiting make sure to figure out your order or you’ll be faced with half a dozen questions at the counter (which was exactly what happened to me the first time around).

life from my kitchen in Hamburg.

There’s no seating inside, so you’ll have to enjoy your bagel on a park bench or on the go. If you do want to sit down, go to the Russ & Daughters cafe instead, also located in the Lower East Side. But it is the shop that has been around for over a hundred years and is considered the legend, so do check it out. Apart from bagels that are, of course, heavenly (the amount of cream cheese is extremely generous), I also tried their seven-layer halwa. It’s superb and makes for a great edible souvenir to bring from New York.

## Kossar’s Bagels and Bialys

Another great place if you are looking for bagels is Kossar’s Bagels and Bialys that has been continuously running since 1936. Their original location was in the Lower East Side but, unfortunately, didn’t survive. The new bakery opened its doors in 1960 in the same neighborhood and you can still find it on Grand Street, all those years later.

I tried their everything bagel with pastrami, egg and cheese which was fantastic, but their specialty is actually bialys which were brought to New York by the Polish immigrants. Bialy originally comes from the city of Białystok in Poland and is a traditional bread roll in Polish Ashkenazi Jewish cuisine.

Bialys are similar to bagels in that they are made from the same dough, but they are not boiled beforehand. The shape also differs: bialys are pressed and stretched into a round with a small depression in the middle which is usually filled with caramelized onions.

## Essex Market

One of the best ways to find a big variety of delicious and affordable meals in New York is by hitting one of its markets. Essex Market is one of the best places to eat in the Lower East Side. It has a history that stretches back as far as 1818 when dozens of independent pushcart peddlers sold all kinds of foods under open sky in LES.

When the streets became too crowded with pushcarts, a series of indoor markets was created In New York and one of them was Essex Street Market that featured close to 500 vendors. The year was 1940.

Over the next decades the market went through financial troubles, a relocation within the neighborhood, and major renovations. Today, Essex Market is located in a newly-renovated building at the intersection of Essex and Delancey streets. It’s modern, spacious, with a sun-lit mezzanine. Not overcrowded like Chelsey Market and it’s always easy to find a table to have your meal.

I’ve tried Unregular Pizza and Zerza Moroccan at the market both of which were great. A few other shops and restaurants that were on my radar but I didn’t have the time to try them: Sugar Sweet Sunshine bakery (try their banana pudding), Kotti Berliner Döner Kebab (given that I live in Germany, it didn’t make sense to eat kebab, but it looked good), and Nordic Preserves.

## Xi’an Famous Foods

Xi’an Famous Foods is hands down one of my favorite places to eat in the Lower East Side (and New York at large because they have many locations). I never miss a chance to devour their (indeed) famous hand-pulled noodles when I visit.

The restaurant was launched by Jason Wang and his father David, Chinese immigrants from the city of Xi’an, back in 2015 and has grown into a chain of 14 locations all over New York. If you are exploring the Lower East Side, check out their location in China Town.

As the business grew, the high quality stayed the same: they still make their own chili oil and hand pull noodles to order. I love how simple and down-to-earth their restaurants are. The space is usually small, featuring an open kitchen so you can watch the cooking process. Pretty much every branch always has a line of people waiting, but it moves really fast.

Be aware that most dishes are quite spicy, bold flavors are their signature. Spicy Cumin Lamb Noodles is, probably, their most popular dish: wide hand-ripped noodles are mixed with slices of spicy cumin lamb and Xi’an’s own soy and black rice vinegar sauce.

## Yonah Schimmel’s Knish Bakery

This iconic bakery in the Lower East Side is so unassuming you could easily pass it by on the street. And that would be unfortunate because it is the last remaining knish bakery in Manhattan.

It was opened by Yonah Schimmel, a Romanian rabbi, in 1910 and the original shop remains on East Houston Street to this day. The current owner is Yonah’s great nephew which makes it a family-run business, over a hundred years later.

A knish (k is pronounced) is a snack brought to New York by Ashkenazi Jewish immigrants in the early 20th century. It consists of creamy mashed potatoes wrapped in thin dough and baked. The fillings can vary, at Yonah Schimmel’s Bakery, for example, you can find knishes with cabbage, kasha, mushrooms and spinach, but potato is definitely the most popular one.

Some of the most notable customers of the bakery include Eleanor Roosevelt, Barbara Streisand, Woody Allen, Evan Rachel Wood and Martha Stewart, to name a few.

I’d say this is a good place to eat in the Lower East Side if you are already in the neighborhood but more so for its history rather than exceptional taste of knishes. The potato knish I tried was ok, but a bit bland to my taste. So if you are exploring the Lower East Side, stop by to try it for yourself, but I wouldn’t make a trip out here just for the knishes.

## Erin Mckenna’s Bakery

Erin Mckenna’s Bakery has been creating gluten-free and vegan goods since 2005. The bakery in the Lower East Side is their original location. They have since opened 3 more locations in the U.S.

All of their baked goods are free from wheat, gluten, dairy, eggs and soy. They also avoid nuts in their products (except for coconut), but their flour of choice (Bob’s Red Mill) might have traces of nuts and soy — so ask at the bakery what’s the safest choice for you would be, if you have an allergy. As for sweeteners, agave nectar and evaporated cane juice are used in the desserts.

While I don’t have an allergy, I do try to avoid gluten, when possible, so it was great to find this place just around the corner from our Airbnb. They have all kinds of sweet and savory goods: from cupcakes and brownies to biscuits and bagels. Regardless whether you are following a gluten-free or vegan diet or not, you’ll be surprised by how good their stuff is.

Still not convinced? Here’s another reason to visit this bakery: it was used as a filming location for Gossip Girl!

## Vita Coffee

This was, hands down, some of the best coffee I’ve had in New York. A tiny dark coffee shop right next door to our Airbnb turned out to be so fantastic we had our morning cappuccinos here almost every day of the trip. Vita Coffee, as it turned out, is an established brand from Seattle.

They work directly with coffee farmers around the world and have been roasting the beans in Seattle since 1995 on vintage German machines (I guess that’s a good thing? In any case, sounds cool!). Not the least important is that the coffee is prepared by award-winning baristas. They have multiple locations in Seattle and only two in New York, one in Brooklyn and one in the Lower East Side.

The space is quite small and there’s no indoor sitting so it’s best to get a coffee to go.

### And these are all the places to eat in the Lower East Side I had the time to try out. I hope you enjoy exploring LES and eating your way through it as much as I did.
