title: The Best Cafes, Coffee, Brunch & Bakeries in SoHo NYC • The Wanderbug
author: Genevieve Lauren
text:
*Welcome to The Wanderbug, a travel blog written for humans, by a human. I'm Genevieve, and every guide is personally written by me and based on my firsthand travel experiences.*

SoHo is one of the most stylish neighbourhoods in New York City, which makes it one of the city’s great brunch & cafe hotspots. After living next to SoHo (in Nolita) for nearly two years, I’ve put together this guide to **the best cafes, brunch spots, coffee & bakeries in SoHo,** based on my own personal experience. 

I’ve included some old school institutions like **Balthazar **(fancy) and **Landmark Diner**(no frills!), as well as new wave cafes and coffee shops like **Jack’s Wife Freda** (a favourite!), **La Mercerie **and Matchaful. 

Read on for the complete lowdown on the best brunch & cafes in SoHo, as well as the best places to get good coffee, and excellent baked treats!

**Love SoHo?** Check out my SoHo Neighbourhood guide for a complete & succinct guide to the highlights of the neighbourhood, including the best things to do in SoHo, best shopping & best places to eat and drink. For more details on SoHo’s best restaurants, check out my complete guide to the best restaurants & diners in SoHo.

**Planning a trip to New York City?**Check out my complete New York City Travel Guide on Rexby, to download a map with more than 140+ saved locations for the best things to do, see, eat & discover in New York City.

## Best Cafes & Brunch Spots in SoHo

### Balthazar

Balthazar is a SoHo institution, which opened in 1997 and one of the most legendary of Keith McNally’s hotspots. Balthazar is a French brasserie, yet it’s got an unmistakable New York City vibe – perfect for your first trip to New York City.

Balthazar does **brunch on weekends**, and it’s arguably even more of a scene than it is at dinner! Balthazar’s brunch menu pulls out all the stops, with classic dishes likes eggs benedict, omelettes and croque madame, as well as an oyster bar, and restaurant-style starters and entrees (mains), like goat cheese & onion tart, steak tartare, chicken paillard, macaroni au gratin and the classic Balthazar cheeseburger.

*Address: 80 Spring St, New York*

### Jack’s Wife Freda

Jack’s Wife Freda is one my favourite cafes in all of New York City, and one of the best brunch spots in SoHo.

It’s a charming SoHo cafe with a Mediterranean and Middle Eastern inspired all-day menu, featuring fresh takes on brunch classics, like **rosewater waffles** and **green shakshuka**, along with sandwiches, salads and mains. 

It’s a quintessential New York City brunch spot, with locations in SoHo, West Village and Chelsea. It was my go-to brunch spot when we lived nearby.

*Address: 226 Lafayette St, New York*

### La Mercerie

La Mercerie is one of the best brunch spots in SoHo, and the **chicest cafe in New York City. **

With interiors by legendary New York City design studio **Roman & Williams**, La Mercerie is a gorgeous French cafe, helmed by classically trained chef Marie-Aude Rose. 

La Mercerie has a boulangerie, as well as classic French brunch dishes like crepes, salmon tartine and ouefs cocotte. Don’t miss the adjacent **furniture & interiors store**, before you go.

*Address: 53 Howard St, New York*

### St Ambroeus Lafayette

St Ambroeus is a stylish Milanese restaurant with a handful of locations across Manhattan and the Hamptons. The SoHo outpost, St Ambroeus Lafayette, has a tightly curated breakfast and brunch menu, and is the perfect spot for an elegant start to the day in downtown Manhattan.

*Address: 265 Lafayette St, New York*

## Best Diners in SoHo

Diners are a dying breed in New York City, but you can still find a couple of diners in SoHo. One is a no-frills, old school institution Landmark Diner, and the other is the new-school, retro glam SoHo Diner. Two very different diner experiences!

### SoHo Diner

SoHo Diner is one of the most Instagrammable brunch spots in New York City. Located in the SoHo Grand Hotel, SoHo Diner is a glam diner with a retro flair and serves an extensive menu of brunch classics. **It’s a bit of a scene**, especially during fashion week, but it’s a fun spot.

*Address: 320 W Broadway, New York*

### Landmark Coffee Shop & Pancake House

Step back in time at Landmark Coffee Shop & Pancake House, a genuine, **no-frills New York City diner. **This is a New York City diner of yesteryear, serving simple diner classics like **grilled cheese, corned hash** and **chocolate chip pancakes. **This is probably one of the only places in SoHo that you’ll find a meal under $10.

*Address: 158 Grand St, New York*

## Best Coffee Shops in SoHo

As an Australian living in New York City, I made it my mission to find the best Aussie-style coffee in the city. Luckily, good coffee can be found all over SoHo!

### Ground Support Cafe

Ground Support Cafe does some of the best coffee in SoHo, and has been a neighbourhood hangout for over a decade. It has a welcoming, laidback vibe which can be a breath of fresh air in high maintenance SoHo. It was my go-to coffee spot in SoHo, when I lived nearby.

*Address: 399 W Broadway, New York*

### Matchaful

Off the coffee? Matchaful is a trendy matcha cafe in SoHo, offering ceremonial-grade Matcha lattes, along with a range of health bites and snacks. It’s one of the best spots for a healthy bite or take out in SoHo.

*Address: 184 Prince St, New York*

### La Colombe

La Colombe’s outpost on Lafayette St is a reliable spot for great coffee in SoHo.

*Address: 154 Price St, New York*

## Best Bakeries in SoHo

It might seem surprising, but SoHo is full of excellent bakeries – something that isn’t exactly easy to come by in New York City. Of course, being SoHo, all of the best bakeries are fairly luxurious.

### Balthazar Bakery

I can honestly still remember the moment I first tried a chocolate doughnut from Balthazar Bakery, TEN YEARS AGO.

This tiny bakery is adjacent to the Balthazar restaurant, and you’ll be able to spot it by the queue winding out the door and down the block. It’s worth the wait, and the line moves quite quickly – be prepared with your order before you get to the front. The pastries, baguettes and the doughnuts are divine.

*Address: 80 Spring St, New York*

### Vesuvio Bakery SoHo

Vesuvio Bakery is the most charming bakery in SoHo, with old world Italian vibes. This gorgeous SoHo bakery has a hundred years of history on Prince Street in SoHo, and has been brought back to life by new owner by Adam Block, who has restored the bakery to its original glory. So cute!

*Address: 160 Spring St, SoHo*

### Dominique Ansel

Try the world-famous**cronut **at the source, at Dominique Ansel. Even today, you’ll still face a lengthy queue to get your hands on the buttery, flaky, croissant-doughnut hybrid. 

Beyond the cronut, find French pastry classics like financiers and Kougin Amanns, and new innovations like Dominique Ansel’s kiwi sorbet bar.

*Address: 189 Spring St, New York*

### Laduree SoHo

Laduree is an iconic Parisian patisserie, with luxurious outposts all over the world – including SoHo. Stop by the pretty salon & tea room for a sweet treat after a morning of shopping in SoHo.

*Address: 398 W Broadway, New York*

## Summary

In summary, the best cafes and brunch spots in SoHo include **Balthazar, La Mercerie, Jack’s Wife Freda **and **St Ambroeus.** 

You can still find diners in SoHo, whether at the old school **Landmark Coffee Shop **or glam, new **SoHo Diner.** There are a number of great bakeries in SoHo, including historic **Vesuvio Bakery**, viral **Dominique Ansel, Balthazar Bakery **and even an outpost of **Laduree**.** Ground Support Cafe** has the best coffee in SoHo, but you can find alternatives like matcha, at **Matchaful.**

title: Tribeca Citizen | Crowd Sourcing: Where do you go to work in the neighborhood?
author: J December
text:
So I needed spot to work for a few hours — too much access to Christmas cookies and other distractions and did not do so well. Here’s where I went, and where I considered going. Curious what else folks have figured out.

I am not counting the coffee shops, since I wanted a good three-hour block. But I have gotten some work done at Laughing Man and Kaffe south.

**New Amsterdam Library | The New York Public Library**

9 Murray

Monday to Thursday, 10a to 7p

Friday and Saturday, 10a to 5p

The library was packed when I went so I left. Nearly every seat was taken and I wanted one of the hightops on the south side, so I could face the wall and not another patron.

UPSIDE: Quiet and conducive to work

DOWNSIDE: No eating or drinking

**Battery Park City Library | The New York Public Library**

175 North End Avenue at Murray

Monday and Wednesday, 10a to 6p

Tuesday and Thursday, 11a to 7p

Friday and Saturday, 10a to 5p

UPSIDE: Quiet and conducive to work

DOWNSIDE: No eating or drinking. A bit smelly

**Poet’s House**

10 River Terrace at Murray

Tuesday to Saturday, 10a to 7p

I have a friend who worked here regularly pre-pandemic. Will try it soon.

**Whole Foods Cafe**

Upstairs on the highway side

7a to 10p, seven days

UPSIDE: Snack access, some outlets for charging

DOWNSIDE: It was kind of a nightmare up here. Babies crying, people playing their phones out loud, talking on the phone. There were seats, but the only one that gave you some isolation were the few on the north windows

**Hudson Eats**

Upstairs at the Winter Garden in Brookfield Place

Monday to Saturday, 10a to 8p

UPSIDE: Food nearby and great views

DOWNSIDE: No outlets, noise

**Brookfield Place**

Upstairs from the Vesey side of the shopping mall

I think the mall closes at 8p??

UPSIDE: Quiet and comfortable with cushy chairs; no one is up there

DOWNSIDE: No outlets.

I love the Roxy Hotel – it’s quiet, good wifi, bathrooms and optional food from Jack’s or the hotel!

Ole & Steen has a quiet basement room that’s always empty – downside no windows, but quiet, good coffee and food, close to everything

Trinity place can be a nice place to hang out – but it is more of a public setting.

I enjoy going to split eights in FIdi – very quiet, good coffee but minimal snacks!

I find that Kaffe North is actually more conducive to getting work done, although you’ll need a personal hotspot. It’s more quiet *because* they don’t offer guest wifi.

There’s a number of coworking spaces that offer one-off drop-ins for a couple of hours or for the day.

– The row of seating outside Hutch and Waldo / Jack’s Hair Salon

– 2nd floor Starbucks on Dey St

– Jack’s Stir Brew Coffee on Reade St

– PAC Lounge

– Conrad Hotel Lobby

– Joe & The Juice in Oculus / Brookfield connection

– Frenchette Bakery, Takahachi Bakery

– Della’s in the early afternoon?

I’ve been meaning to check out Trinity Commons and see if they offer any space just to work / study.

Wow, realizing how much third place spaces we’ve lost in the neighborhood over the years.

Arlo Hotel on Hudson street is pretty chill.

title: Top 8 Best Study Spots in New York City - BookScouter Blog

text:
Looking for the perfect study spot in the hustle and bustle of 📍NYC? Look no further!

In this blog, we will explore the **top 8 best study spots in New York City**. Whether you’re a student, a freelancer, or just someone seeking a quiet place to work, NYC has a plethora of options to suit every need. From cozy coffee shops to stunning libraries, prepare to discover the most amazing study spots that will inspire productivity and fuel your creativity. So grab your books, laptops, or notebooks, and get ready to explore the exciting world of study spots in the Big Apple!

### Think Coffee

**📍***Check **here** to find the nearest Think Coffee cafe *

For those who prefer a more traditional coffee shop setting, Think Coffee is a popular choice among students. With several locations throughout the city, Think Coffee offers a laid-back atmosphere, delicious coffee, and a variety of seating options. Whether you prefer a quiet corner or a communal table, you’ll find a spot that suits your study needs.

### NY Public Library

**📍***476 5th Ave, New York, NY 10018*

🕙*Monday, Thursday – Saturday 10:00 am – 6:00 pm | Tuesday and Wednesday 10:00 am – 8:00 pm | Sunday 1:00 pm – 5:00 pm*

No list of study spots in NYC would be complete without mentioning the iconic NY Public Library, where you’ll find yourself immersed in a world of knowledge. With its grand architecture and extensive collection, this library offers a serene environment for focused studying. The reading rooms are equipped with study tables, power outlets, and free Wi-Fi, making it an ideal spot for students seeking a quiet and distraction-free space. By the way, the Rose Main Reading Room, with its high ceilings and abundant natural light, is highly popular among college students.

### The Metropolitan Museum of Art

**📍***1000 5th Ave, New York, NY 10028*

🕙*Sunday – Tuesday and Thursday 10:00 am – 5:00 pm | Wednesday closed | Friday and Saturday 10:00 am – 9:00 pm*

If you’re looking for a study spot that offers the perfect blend of tranquility and inspiration, the Metropolitan Museum of Art is your choice. With its vast collection of art and artifacts, this museum provides a unique study environment. Whether you find a quiet corner in the museum’s many galleries or choose to work in the peaceful courtyard, you’ll find yourself surrounded by beauty and culture.

### Housing Works Bookstore Cafe

**📍***126 Crosby St, New York, NY 10012*

🕙*Monday – Sunday 11:00 am – 8:00 pm*

For a unique study spot with a literary twist, head to the Housing Works Bookstore Cafe in SoHo. This bookstore offers a quiet atmosphere, comfortable seating, and a wide selection of books to browse during your study breaks. The best part? All proceeds go towards supporting the Housing Works charity, which helps homeless New Yorkers living with HIV/AIDS.

### Columbia University Libraries

**📍***535 W 114th St, New York, NY 10027*

🕙*Monday – Thursday 9:00 am – 9:00 pm | Friday 9:00 am – 6:00 pm | Saturday 11:00 am – 6:00 pm | Sunday 12:00 pm – 9:00 pm*

If you’re a student or affiliated with Columbia University, their libraries are a haven for focused studying. The Butler Library, with its vast collection and variety of study spaces, is a favorite among students. The library offers quiet study rooms, group study areas, and even a designated silent study floor.

### The High Line

**📍***Gansevoort St. To W. 30 St. bet. Washington St. and 11 Ave. Manhattan, New York, NY 10011*

🕙*Monday – Sunday 7:00 am – 10:00 pm*

🏆*Best outdoor study spot*

If you enjoy studying outdoors, The High Line offers a unique and refreshing experience. This elevated park and walking trail provide stunning views of the city, along with ample seating and greenery. Find a quiet spot on one of the park’s benches, or bring a blanket to spread out on the grass. Studying in nature can help boost creativity and focus, making it a great option for students looking for a change of scenery.

### Ace Hotel Lobby

**📍***20 W 29th St, New York, NY 10001*

🕙*Sunday – Wednesday 7:30 am – 11:30 pm | Thursday – Saturday 7:30 am – 12:30 am*

🏆*Best late-night study spot*

Located in the heart of Manhattan, the Ace Hotel Lobby offers a unique and stylish study space. With its cozy ambiance and comfortable seating, it’s the perfect spot to dive into your textbooks. The free Wi-Fi and the availability of coffee and snacks make it even more appealing for students looking to get some serious studying done.

### Elmer Holmes Bobst Library

**📍***70 Washington Square S, New York, NY 10012*

🕙*Open at all times*

🏆*Best 24/7 hour study spot*

Located in the heart of New York University’s campus, this iconic library offers a tranquil and productive environment for students to focus and concentrate. With its vast collection of books, journals, and digital resources, Bobst Library provides ample materials for research and studying. The library boasts a variety of study spaces, including individual carrels, group study rooms, and comfortable seating areas, ensuring that every student can find their ideal spot.

## Best Study Spots in New York City: Final Thoughts

In a city as vibrant as New York, finding the perfect study spot, places to sell used books in New York City, the cutest coffee, or the funniest bars is not easy, but essential for students looking for excellent college years.

As for study spots, whether you prefer the cozy ambiance of a hotel lobby, the quiet elegance of a library, or the inspiration of an art museum, these **8 study spots in NYC** offer something for everyone. So grab your books, find your spot, and get ready to conquer your exams with ease in the incredible city that never sleeps.

title: Tribeca Neighborhood Guide: Where to Eat, Drink & Stay
author: Catrina S
publication: Brooklyn's Lifestyle | An Insider Travel Guide to NYC
text:
A field guide to the Tribeca neighborhood as it actually functions today, from the quiet residential blocks west of Hudson to the cultural grid that defines its modern identity.

QUICK FACTS

- **The Two Tribecas:**West of Hudson Street is residential. East of Hudson is the commercial spine.
- **Best For:**Second‑visit travelers who want a neighborhood with real texture, festival‑week New Yorkers who know how to avoid Midtown gridlock, and anyone who prefers a controlled downtown circuit over the chaos of SoHo or the West Village.
- **Main Transit:**1 [Franklin Street, Canal Street, Chambers Street]. A C E [Canal Street]. 2 3 [Chambers Street].
- **Price Point:**$$$$.

## The Tribeca Neighborhood at a Glance

Tribeca is the most expensive defense mechanism in New York. Belgian blocks. Converted textile lofts. Residents who pay five‑figure rents for the privilege of being left alone. The neighborhood is engineered for privacy, which is why most visitors mistake it for quiet to the point of dull.

It is not. Tribeca is one of the rare downtown enclaves whose architecture has not been retrofitted for foot traffic. The sidewalks remain cobblestone. The buildings remain industrial. The streets are wide enough that you can hear your own footsteps. The cast‑iron facades and textile-mill proportions are the physical evidence of a neighborhood that decided in the 1990s that it would tolerate visitors but never perform for them. That is the difference between Tribeca and SoHo, three blocks north, where every storefront has been retrofitted for tourism.

This guide is built for year‑round Tribeca. The seasonal anchors, the June festival, the fall gallery openings, and the deep‑winter quiet live in the Through the Year section below.

## The Position

**What changed**: Tribeca has spent the last decade absorbing the city’s most expensive cultural infrastructure. Galleries moving down from Chelsea. A wave of restaurant openings around the **Walker Hotel**. A continued conversion of pre‑2008 office stock into residential lofts. The neighborhood now functions as a self‑contained downtown enclave rather than a corridor between SoHo and FiDi.

**The mistake people make:** Assuming Tribeca is interchangeable with SoHo. It is not. SoHo is built for foot traffic and has been since the 1990s. Tribeca is built for residents and has not changed that posture for more than thirty years.

**Who this is for: **Second-visit New Yorkers who want a downtown circuit without the West Village crowds. Festival-goers during the June window. Anyone who values controlled curation over open chaos.

# The 3×3

## Three Eats

### The Iconic — The Odeon

📍 Location: **145 West Broadway — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **The Odeon**

Trying to land a dinner reservation here on a Friday or Saturday is a fool’s errand. Prime‑time tables are monopolized by studio dinners during the festival and industry tables the rest of the year. Aim for the bar at 11 PM. The neon-lit room is the birthplace of the neighborhood’s creative identity, and the bar is the most reliable seat in the city for an unsolicited celebrity sighting over a martini and fries.

### The New [2026] — Seventy Seven Alley

📍 Location: **28 Cortlandt Alley — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **Seventy Seven Alley**

** **Tribeca’s only confirmed 2026 opening with enough weight to anchor this slot. A chef-driven studio inside the **Walker Hotel**, built around elemental flavor architecture and a counter that reads more like a working atelier than a dining room. It is the rare “new” Tribeca restaurant that feels of the neighborhood rather than imported for it.

### The Secret — Bubby’s

📍 Location: **|120 Hudson Street — Tribeca, Manhattan**  🌐 Website: **Bubby’s**

Skip weekend brunch. The line of out‑of‑towners stretches down the block. Go on a Tuesday at 3 PM for a slice of sour cherry pie and a cold brew when the dining room exhales.

If you actually want weekend brunch in Tribeca, walk three blocks east to **Two Hands [251 Church Street]**. The sun-drenched, health-conscious antidote to the tourist-clogged line outside Bubby’s. While out-of-towners wait on the hot pavement for dense pancakes, locals drift to this airy, Australian-inspired room on Church Street, removed from the festival gridlock and entirely its own rhythm.

Order the Pesto Feta Scramble [soft ribboned eggs, white balsamic, macadamia nut pesto on thick sourdough] with a flawless flat white. A light, high-execution alternative that fuels the Architecture Walk without the food coma.

## Three Drinks

### Coffee — Laughing Man Coffee

📍 Location: **184 Duane Street — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **Laughing Man Coffee**

** **Hugh Jackman’s tiny, sidewalk-facing espresso window right off Duane Park. No indoor seating. That is the point. Grab a flat white and sit on a park bench across the cobblestones to watch the neighborhood wake up.

### Cocktail — Smith & Mills

📍 Location: **71 North Moore Street — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **Smith & Mills**

** **A windowless, converted carriage house that feels removed from the grid. It holds a handful of tables and fills up instantly. The dark-wood interior is the right room for a quiet, late-night cocktail in any season.

### Third Space — The Ear Inn

📍 Location: **326 Spring Street — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **The Ear Inn**

Technically, the border of Tribeca and Hudson Square. One of the oldest continuously operating taverns in the city. Loud, unpretentious, sawdust-strewn. If your goal is to escape downtown pretense entirely, this is the room, any night of the year.

**Three more worth knowing: **For serious coffee, **Interlude** [145 Hudson Street] is the upgrade. **WarrenPeace [77 Warren Street]**, a candlelit Mediterranean cocktail bar built for late, unhurried evenings. And **Holywater [112 Reade Street]**, a subterranean room designed for the cold months. Neither displaces the three above; both are the right call when those are full.

## Three Activities

### Cultural — Spring Studios

📍 Location: **50 Varick Street — Tribeca, Manhattan**

The Tribeca Festival’s nominal home, but the year-round programming is the under-recognized story: live podcasts, creator panels, the Tribeca Storytelling Summit, and a steady run of industry events. Even outside festival weeks, the sidewalk in front of the building functions as an informal hub for the city’s independent film and storytelling community.

### Outdoor — Duane Park

📍 Location: **Duane and Hudson Streets — Tribeca, Manhattan**

** **The small, cobblestoned green at the residential heart of west-of-Hudson Tribeca. Before 9 AM on any weekday, it is the quietest seat in the neighborhood. Bring a coffee from Laughing Man and watch the residents walk their dogs before the day starts.

### Architecture Walk — West-of-Hudson Loop

Tribeca’s defining feature is its loft architecture. Most visitors drive through the neighborhood instead of walking it. Start at North Moore, loop down Hudson, cut across Franklin, and finish at Duane Park. The Belgian blocks, cast-iron facades, and textile-mill proportions tell the story better than any gallery roster.

## The Local Habit

For residents, Tribeca morning is built around architectural quiet. Before 9 AM, the residential streets west of Hudson are nearly empty. Locals walk dogs along the cobblestones of Hudson Street between Duane and Franklin, get an espresso at **Laughing Man [184 Duane Street]** with no line, and sit at Duane Park for ten minutes before the day starts. The point is the walk. Belgian blocks. Quiet streets. The version of Tribeca that exists when nobody is filming in it. During festival weeks, the cafés on Varick get gridlocked by 8:30 AM, but the residential interior holds its rhythm year-round.

The newest wrinkle in the weekend version of this ritual is **Meadow Lane [355 Greenwich Street]**, the gourmet grocer that opened in late 2025 and promptly drew lines down the block. It is very good: the prepared foods, the Grandma’s meatballs, the florals, and it is also a $65 olive-oil spectacle that tells you something about where the neighborhood is heading. Go early on a Saturday, before the line forms, and treat it as provisioning rather than theater. Whether it reads as fixture or symptom depends on the morning.

## Spas in Tribeca

Tribeca’s spa density tells you something about who actually lives here. The neighborhood is one of the few in Manhattan where you can walk five blocks and pass three serious wellness rooms. Residents recover here. That is part of the residential identity, not an add-on.

**AIRE Ancient Baths [88 Franklin Street]** is the destination, 16,000 square feet inside a restored 1883 textile factory, candlelit baths at four temperatures [hot plunge at 104°F, cold plunge at 55°F, tepidarium at 97°F, flotarium at 98°F], with an expanded footprint at 84 Franklin as of summer 2025. Book a Friday afternoon and leave the neighborhood three hours later, recovered.

**Tribeca Spa of Tranquility [462 Greenwich Street]** has been on this stretch since 2005. The Korean body scrub is the signature; W magazine called it one of the most distinctive treatments in the world. Less theatrical than AIRE, more like a neighborhood doctor’s office for tension.

**La Réserve Aesthetics Med Spa + Wellness [177 Duane Street]** is the med-spa hybrid—full-spectrum infrared sauna, cold plunge, and IV therapy alongside Botox and dermal fillers. The afternoon-recovery option for residents who treat wellness as preventive medicine.

## Where to Stay

Tribeca’s hotel inventory is small but unusually layered. The neighborhood has fewer than ten named properties, but those properties span the prestige spectrum from De Niro-owned to recent boutique, and they all sit within a six-block radius.

### The Iconic — The Greenwich Hotel

📍 Location: **377 Greenwich Street — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **The Greenwich Hotel**

Robert De Niro’s flagship hotel. Eighty-eight rooms hidden behind an unmarked brick facade on a quiet block of Greenwich Street. The Greenwich is industry shorthand for downtown discretion. Private entries. A members-only Drawing Room. The copper-lined pool at **Shibui Spa** that you have already seen in a year of magazine spreads. This is what “Tribeca hotel” means in shorthand, built for residents who happen to be in town for a few days, not for tourists who happen to land in the neighborhood.

### The New — Walker Hotel Tribeca

📍 Location: **77 Walker Street — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **Walker Hotel Tribeca**

The hotel that anchors **Seventy Seven Alley**, Tribeca’s most talked-about new dining room. Walker does not perform prestige the way The Greenwich does. It operates inside it. The lobby reads as a working space rather than a stage set, and the room rate sits hundreds of dollars below the Greenwich for materially the same neighborhood access. For the second-visit traveler who has done The Greenwich, Walker is the right swap.

### The Secret — Smyth Tribeca

📍 Location: **85 West Broadway — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **Smyth Tribeca**

The Thompson-affiliated property that rarely gets written about. Roughly one hundred rooms on the corner of Chambers Street and West Broadway, a stretch few travelers think to consider Tribeca. The Smyth is purpose-built for the visitor who wants Tribeca’s quiet without paying for its prestige. The location puts you closer to BMCC and Brookfield Place than to Greenwich Street, which is either the right or wrong tradeoff depending on what you are here to do.

**If you cannot get a Tribeca room: **walk west into Hudson Square [**Hotel Barrière Fouquet’s** is the obvious upgrade], or south into FiDi [**The Beekman** is the prestige play. The **Conrad Downtown** is the all-suite play. Both neighborhoods sit within a ten-minute walk of west-of-Hudson Tribeca.

# TriBeca Through the Year

## June: The Festival Window [June 3–14, 2026]

For two weeks in June, the architectural armor cracks open. The 25th Anniversary Tribeca Festival draws an influx of global industry badges, red-carpet barricades, and corporate activations that rewrite the neighborhood’s flow. There are essentially two Tribecas in early June. West of Hudson Street is the residential enclave, quiet by design. East of Hudson is the festival grid, credentialed, ticketed, surveilled.

**Spring Studios [50 Varick Street]** is the physical center of gravity, but only for the festival’s live podcasts, creator panels, and the Tribeca Storytelling Summit. The actual screening hubs sit elsewhere: the **OKX Theater at BMCC [199 Chambers Street]**, the **SVA Theatre in Chelsea**, **Village East by Angelika**, the **AMC 19th Street**, and the **Beacon Theatre** uptown for opening night. If you booked a screening ticket assuming everything sits within a four-block walk, plan for an Uber.

**The Rush Ticket Rule: **Lines form one hour before each screening. Empty seats are surrendered to the Rush Ticket standby line 10 minutes before the lights go down. Do not show up late.

**Festival-week-only skip: **The Hudson River Park Piers [25 & 26]. They become primary real estate for corporate sponsor step-and-repeats and private afterparties. Walk ten minutes south to Battery Park City instead.

## September–October: Gallery Season

Tribeca’s gallery district concentrates on Walker, White, and Franklin Streets. Major openings run mid-September through the second week of October, when the Chelsea-to-Tribeca migration of the last decade is most visible. Three anchors are worth planning around.

**55 Walker Street **is the cluster’s center of gravity. Three serious contemporary programs share the building: Bortolami, Kaufmann Repetto, and Andrew Kreps. Kaufmann Repetto [Italian-rooted, internationally networked] runs the most consistent calendar. If you see one show in Tribeca, start here.

**R & Company [82 Franklin Street]** is the design-and-objects anchor: collectible twentieth- and twenty-first-century furniture and contemporary commissions, the kind of pieces that do not surface at a fair booth. The gallery has been on Franklin since 2000 and expanded to a second space on White Street. The catalog is built, not curated, by season.

For fashion adjacent to the galleries, **La Garçonne** **[465 Greenwich Street]** is the first physical store from the long-running online retailer. It reads more like a curated project space than a shop. The editorial restraint matches the galleries around it. The cooler weather also makes the Architecture Walk most accessible; Belgian blocks are less punishing in October than in July. If you have time for one cultural beat in Tribeca outside of festival weeks, this is the window.

## December–February: The Quiet Tribeca

The case for visiting Tribeca in deep winter is the case for the neighborhood at its truest. Tourism is low. The festival is six months away, and the residential character is at its most pronounced. The streets are empty. The restaurants take walk-ins. The Odeon’s bar is the warmest room in the city on a cold Tuesday. The Architecture Walk works year-round but reads differently in winter. And the cast-iron facades feel more industrial, less postcard. This is the Tribeca residents protect when they sign their leases.

## The 2026 Pulse

Tribeca’s 2026 story is a convergence of four forces: a festival that has outgrown its footprint, a dining revival anchored by new hotel-adjacent openings, a quiet but meaningful shift in the built environment south of Chambers, and a recalibration of the waterfront’s role.

**The Festival Has Decentralized.** The 25th Anniversary Tribeca Festival is now a citywide organism. Opening night at the Beacon Theatre, major screenings in Chelsea and the East Village, and a lineup heavy with world premieres and live performances signal a structural shift: Tribeca is the brand, not the container.

**Dining Is Reasserting Itself.** Seventy Seven Alley’s March 2026 debut marks a deliberate push to fuse culinary and arts programming in a single walkable circuit. The restaurant’s gallery-influenced design and tasting-studio format reflect a broader downtown recalibration toward experiential dining. Faux [the late-night, two-level project from George McNally, aiming to open July 2026] reinforces the return of a social, after-hours Tribeca. The kitchen will be led by Chef Kristina Ramos, formerly of Eleven Madison Park and Oxalis.

**The Built Environment Is Shifting at the Edges.** 25 Park Row’s ongoing residential consolidation continues to reshape the southern boundary between Tribeca and FiDi, part of a larger wave of downtown conversions accelerated by 2026 tax-incentive deadlines. While not a Tribeca address, the pressure radiates north: more residents, more foot traffic, more demand for neighborhood-scale dining and culture.

**The Waterfront Is Entering a New Phase.** Pier 26’s science-focused redevelopment [including the new marine-themed play area] signals a shift toward educational and ecological programming along the Hudson. During festival weeks, this space becomes a staging ground for sponsor activations, further tightening the relationship between the waterfront and the festival grid.

**The Pulse, distilled:** Tribeca in 2026 is no longer the festival’s physical center. It is the narrative center—the name, the memory, the myth. The neighborhood is responding with new dining, new cultural anchors, and a slow architectural evolution that keeps its residential core intact while absorbing the city’s broader downtown revival.

## Curation by Subtraction

### Skip: Locanda Verde

📍 Location: **377 Greenwich Street — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **Locanda Verde**

Robert De Niro’s flagship Italian restaurant at The Greenwich Hotel is booked year-round and industry-owned during the festival. Reservations open four weeks out. The prime slots are gone in seconds. The food is fine; the bottleneck is the calendar.

**Walk three blocks to Walker’s [16 North Moore Street]**, a true neighborhood tavern with French-leaning plates, walk-in friendly, and historically insulated from reservation pressure.

### Skip: Frenchette

📍 Location: **220 Church Street — Tribeca, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **Frenchette**

The high-end French sister to Frenchette Bakery is industry-bound year-round and impossible during the festival. The bakery is excellent; the restaurant is gated during the festival. The bakery is excellent; the restaurant is gated.

Walk three blocks to **Yves** **[385 Greenwich Street]**. Modern French in a 200-year-old former Seafarers Inn, 46 seats inside and outdoor tables wrapping the corner at North Moore.

### Skip: The Westfield WTC Mall

📍 Location: **185 Greenwich Street — Financial District, Manhattan** | 🌐 Website: **The Westfield WTC Mall**

Touristed conflation with Tribeca. The chain-store retail mix has no neighborhood character. The **Oculus** is architecturally interesting for about five minutes. Then you are in a mall.

**Walk three blocks to Korin Japanese Trading [57 Warren Street],** the specialty knife and tableware shop that supplies most of the city’s restaurant kitchens. Or **The Mysterious Bookshop [58 Warren Street]**, the only mystery-specialty bookstore in New York.

## The Escape Route

**Too Crowded**? Walk ten minutes south to Battery Park City. The lawns are wide, the river views are unobstructed, and Tribeca’s residential rhythm gives way to the quieter southern tip of Manhattan.

**Want More**? Take the 1 train north to Christopher Street, and you are in the West Village. Or walk fifteen minutes south from Chambers Street to Wall Street and the new residential FiDi—the neighborhood that has spent 2026 absorbing everything Tribeca cannot.

BKLS PRO-TIP

The Odeon martini-and-fries at 11 PM is the highest-leverage decision in the neighborhood—any night of the year, not just during festival weeks. You skip the impossible-on-most-nights dinner reservation, you arrive after the dinner rush has rolled out, and you get the original room at its truest hour. Order the martini cold and dry. The fries are the standard.

BKLS NOTE

Tribeca does not open itself to outsiders easily. The architecture is the first defense. The price is the second. The residents do not perform for visitors and will not pretend to. To visit well is to accept that—to walk the cobblestones quietly, to eat at the bar instead of insisting on a table, to find the version of the neighborhood that exists when nobody is filming in it.

Tribeca is a vibrant neighborhood in Lower Manhattan, known for its mix of old-school charm and modern city life. The best restaurants in Tribeca cover everything from fancy, chef-run kitchens to cozy cafés and hidden gems serving comfort food.

Whether you’re planning a special night out or just looking for a good place to grab lunch, there’s something here for everyone. In this guide, you’ll find the 10 best restaurants in Tribeca, New York City that everyone should try.

From fancy, award-winning restaurants to small, cozy spots loved by locals, Tribeca has a little bit of everything. Whether you want a special meal or just something tasty and simple, these are the 10 best restaurants in Tribeca that you should definitely try.

## 1. Scalini Fedeli

Scalini Fedeli is often considered one of the best restaurants in Tribeca, offering a refined Italian dining experience with old-world charm. Situated on Duane Street, this elegant establishment offers a quiet escape from the bustling city. The interior is adorned with warm, classic decor, creating an intimate atmosphere perfect for romantic dinners or special occasions. Known for its impeccable service, Scalini Fedeli ensures every guest feels attended to and pampered.

Their menu highlights sophisticated Italian dishes with modern influences. Signature offerings include the Ricotta and Truffle Ravioli, the Veal Chop Milanese, and their delectable Tiramisu. ## Tips for First-Time Visitors to Tribeca Restaurants

Visiting Tribeca for the first time and planning to eat out? This stylish Manhattan neighborhood is famous for its fancy restaurants, cute cafés, and spots run by celebrity chefs. To enjoy your food experience, here are some simple tips:

- **Book Your Table Early**: Popular spots like Locanda Verde, Bubby’s, and The Odeon can get really busy, especially on weekends. It’s smart to make a reservation ahead of time using apps like OpenTable or Resy.
- **Try Hidden Gems Too**: Big-name places are great, but Tribeca also has amazing smaller restaurants that aren’t as well-known. Don’t be afraid to explore a little, you might discover your new favorite spot.
- **Look at the Menu Before You Go**: Menus can change often, especially if the place uses seasonal ingredients. Check the restaurant’s website or social media to see what they’re serving that day.
- **Expect Higher Prices**: Dining in Tribeca isn’t cheap. Keep in mind that prices are higher than average, and don’t forget to include tax and a 20% tip when figuring out your budget.
- **Lunch Can Be a Good Deal**: Want to try a fancy place without breaking the bank? Go for lunch. Many spots have lower-priced lunch specials or fixed-price menus.
- **Ask About Specials**: Many chefs create special dishes that aren’t on the regular menu. Ask your server what’s special that day, you might end up with something amazing.
- **Skip Driving:**Parking in Tribeca is tough and garages are pricey. It’s usually easier to take the subway or grab an Uber or Lyft.
- **Save Room for Dessert**: Tribeca has some seriously good desserts, places like Frenchette and Sarabeth’s are known for them. Don’t miss out!

## FAQs

**What are the best restaurants in Tribeca for fine dining?**

Tribeca offers a range of upscale dining options. Some of the top fine dining spots include “Nobu” for its Japanese-Peruvian fusion, and “The Odeon,” a chic French bistro.

**Where can I find the best Italian food in Tribeca?**

For authentic Italian cuisine, “Lupa Osteria Romana” is a local favourite known for its traditional Roman dishes, while “Parm” offers a modern twist on classic Italian-American comfort food.

**What are the best places for brunch in Tribeca?**

“Bubby’s” is an iconic brunch spot in Tribeca, offering a delicious array of comfort food, while “Teedy’s” is a great choice for a more laid-back, cosy brunch experience.

**Which Tribeca restaurants offer the best views?**

“Manhatta” offers stunning views of the skyline and the Hudson River, while “The River Café” on the Brooklyn waterfront also provides breathtaking views.

**Where can I get the best sushi in Tribeca?**

“Sushi Azabu” offers a top-tier sushi experience in Tribeca, renowned for its high-quality fish and intimate atmosphere.

**What are the best vegan or vegetarian-friendly restaurants in Tribeca?**

“Le Botaniste” is a plant-based, vegan-friendly spot offering an innovative menu, and “Superiority Burger” is another great choice for veggie lovers.

**Are there any family-friendly restaurants in Tribeca?**

“Shake Shack” offers casual American fare perfect for families, and “Tribeca Grill” is a classic family-friendly option with a relaxed atmosphere and diverse menu.

**What are the best casual dining options in Tribeca?**

“The Smith” serves hearty American fare in a lively setting, and “No. 7 Sub” offers delicious sandwiches for a quick and casual meal.

**Which Tribeca restaurants are best for a romantic dinner?**

“La Scaletta” is a cosy, romantic Italian spot, and “Locanda Verde” offers a charming setting and delicious Italian-inspired dishes perfect for a date night.

**What are the best restaurants in Tribeca for a special occasion?**

For special occasions, “Nobu” offers a luxurious dining experience, and “Bouley” (though now closed) was once a renowned spot for upscale celebrations, replaced by newer fine dining locations like “The Greenwich Hotel’s restaurant, The Drawing Room.”

# The 100 Best Restaurants in New York City in 2025 The 100 Best Restaurants

# In New York City 2025

### This year, we’ve named a new No. 1 and added a feature for sharing favorites with friends.

Diners in New York City are spoiled for choice. On a single block, you might find a pizzeria, a noodle shop and a fine-dining institution, all of them stellar. How did we ever narrow more than 20,000 restaurants down to the 100 best?

It was a daunting task.

We started with Pete Wells’s 2024 list and added 100 or so additional places that felt worthy of consideration. Then we hit the streets. (As interim restaurant critics, we — Priya Krishna and Melissa Clark — did the bulk of the eating, with some pinch-hitting by our editor, Brian Gallagher.)

In the past few months, we’ve clocked dozens of hours on the subway and bought several new (larger) pairs of pants. We each returned with winners, then continued to whittle our selections down until we had a list that represented the city’s culinary greatness, across boroughs, cuisines, price points and styles.

Below you’ll see our top 10 restaurants, ranked. After that you’ll see the remaining 90 picks, unranked and listed in alphabetical order. With three of us choosing the restaurants, it was impossible to rank the entire list, as Pete did in years past.

Of course, there are more than 100 amazing restaurants in New York. But these best answered the questions: Where would we send our friends? Which places are worth a splurge? Worth an hourlong subway ride?

Here are our answers to those questions, the 100 best dining experiences to be had in New York City, miracles brought to life by thousands of workers every day.

*This year, use our new checklist feature on each entry to keep track of your favorites and share with friends.*

Ninety more of the best restaurants in New York, listed alphabetically:

## 1. Semma   

 - Indian
- $$$
- 60 Greenwich Avenue
- Greenwich Village, Manhattan
- semma.nyc
- Last reviewed on Jan. 10, 2022

Paul McDonough

New York is teeming with Indian restaurants. Yet before Semma, a deeply personal tribute to the chef Vijay Kumar’s upbringing in the South Indian state of Tamil Nadu, the city’s diners had never seen Indian food like this. Punctuated with chiles, coconut and earthy curry leaves, Semma’s flavors are lingering and loud, yet restrained. Its dosa is the best in the city: a crisp specimen that’s heady with fermentation and slicked with ghee and fiery gunpowder spice. Wisps of steam and the fragrant aromas of peppercorn and star anise waft from the bowls of soup that grace the tables at Old Sport. This minimalist restaurant specializes in Lanzhou beef noodle soup from northwestern China, serving a halal rendition with thin, tensile noodles, a refreshing broth, a sinus-clearing chile crisp and delicate petals of beef and radish. The noodles are pulled to order, the broth made fresh each day, and the flavor deepens with each slurp. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

##  Raf’s   

 - French, Italian
- $$$$
- 290 Elizabeth Street
- NoHo, Manhattan
- rafsnewyork.com
- Last reviewed on July 4, 2023
- ★★

Rachel Vanni for The New York Times

Whether you’re seeking a wonderful plate of pasta, a genial cafe to grab a pastry or simply a chic seat to people watch, Raf’s is the answer. The Elizabeth Street Hospitality Group team transformed a decades-old bakery into a low-lit French Italian restaurant powered by a wood-fired oven and two chefs, Mary Attea and Camari Mick, who bring a stylish flair to classic dishes like escargots, which are enrobed in whipped lardo, and leeks vinaigrette, covered in stretches of stracciatella. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

##  Raku   

 - Japanese
- $$
- 342 East Sixth Street (and one other)
- East Village, Manhattan
- rakunyc.com

Nico Schinco for The New York Times

The chef Norihiro Ishizuka makes his springy udon noodles with uncommon care, each strand an elastic, al dente triumph with a characteristic pinched end. Plunged into bowls of complex, deeply flavored dashi, the noodles harmonize with whichever garnishes Mr. Ishizuka chooses — a dazzling array of delicate tempura, plump nameko mushrooms, pillows of pink crab, shreds of duck. In New York’s Japanese culinary landscape, udon is often overshadowed by ramen and soba. But Raku’s udon empire continues to expand, with three locations in the city and another in Toronto, a testament to both its loyal following and the power of a great noodle. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Randazzo’s Clam Bar   

 - Italian American, Seafood
- $$
- 2017 Emmons Avenue
- Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn
- randazzosclambar.nyc
- Last reviewed on April 23, 2013
- ★

Daniel Krieger for The New York Times

Randazzo’s identifies as a clam bar, but everyone in the know orders the fried calamari. It arrives delicately breaded, fried and greaseless, with a marinara so flavorful and garlicky you’ll want to drink it once the last crunchy squid ring is gone. Prolong the joy by ordering any red-sauced pasta. Spaghetti with the zuppa di pesce comes nicely al dente under a generous jumble of clams, mussels, fish and shrimp, all succulent and perfectly cooked. Of course, as long as you’re here you should also get the clams, littlenecks and cherrystones served raw and ice-cold, the better to magnify their saline splendor. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  S & P Lunch   

 - Diner, Deli, Sandwich
- $$
- 174 Fifth Avenue
- Flatiron, Manhattan
- sandwich.place
- Last reviewed on Dec. 6, 2022
- ★

Lanna Apisukh for The New York Times

The classic luncheonette, with long Formica counters, good tuna melts and servers with pencils behind their ears, is increasingly hard to find around town. Happily, there’s S & P, which has everything you want in an old-school diner, save for the pencils. There are juicy smash burgers, well-built turkey clubs and a dandy egg salad, all properly served with crisp and sour pickles. They’ll even make you a coffee egg cream, which is not one of the flavors I grew up with, but still heartily endorse. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Sailor   

 - American, English, Mediterranean
- $$$$
- 228 DeKalb Avenue
- Fort Greene, Brooklyn
- sailor.nyc
- Last reviewed on Dec. 5, 2023
- ★★★

Evan Sung for The New York Times

April Bloomfield has been helming the stove here in Fort Greene for the past 18 months, quickly establishing Sailor as a standout in a neighborhood of great restaurants. She’s often credited with bringing the British gastro-pub movement stateside, with food that’s understated, direct and full of intense flavors, made with seasonal ingredients and without deferring to fashion or trends. Start with a plate of toast with “green sauce” (a pungent, anchovied salsa verde), then move on to seasonal dishes like pea leaves showered heavily with pecorino, and pork shoulder braised with olives until it practically melts. The sweet-toothed among us pine for Ms. Bloomfield’s British-accented desserts, and the sticky ginger cake soaked in cream is a very fine way to ride Sailor’s wave. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Salty Lunch Lady’s Little Luncheonette   

 - Sandwiches
- $
- 565 Woodward Avenue
- Ridgewood, Queens
- saltylunchlady.com

Star Chefs

How lucky are we that the cafe serving some of New York’s finest sandwiches also offers some of its finest cakes? This corner restaurant in Ridgewood exudes a grandma-esque charm, with slices of peanut-butter-and-jelly cake housed in glass cloches, and mortadella and pickled-pepper sandwiches served on dainty, mismatched floral dinnerware. The chef, Dria Atencio, is an expert in building balance: She salts the jams in her sweets, tosses fried lemons into sandwiches for crunch and acid, and chops cornichons into her mayonnaise. It all tastes like superior home cooking. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

##  Shaw-naé’s House   

 - American, Soul Food
- $$
- 381 Van Duzer Street
- Stapleton Heights, Staten Island
- instagram.com/shawnaeshouse
- Last reviewed on April 2, 2024
- ★★

Colin Clark for The New York Times

If you don’t already live on Staten Island, Shaw-naé Dixon and her cooking will make you feel right at home. Regulars may even get a hug upon entering. The dining room, which has a couple of couches and an electric fireplace in one corner, is equally hospitable. The formidable whole snapper is expertly fried, and the ribs, lacquered with a sweet-and-spicy barbecue sauce, eagerly fall off the bone. Those feeling adventurous (and extremely hungry) should try the “soul fries,” a gonzo take on nachos in which mac and cheese, fried chicken and collard greens are heaped over French fries. The giddy housemade rum punch, served by the pitcher, will help you along. *BRIAN GALLAGHER*

##  Shukette   

 - Middle Eastern
- $$
- 230 Ninth Avenue
- Chelsea, Manhattan
- instagram.com/shukettenyc
- Last reviewed on Sept. 21, 2021

Lanna Apisukh for The New York Times

When Ayesha Nurdjaja seasons a dish, she doesn’t kid around. Shukette’s roster of Middle Eastern dishes vibrate, explode, even gyrate with garlic, lemon, spices and chiles. The hummus, whipped-cream fluffy, is buried under whole chickpeas and pickled onions and bathed with oil; the grilled-to-order laffa (a dinner-plate-size flatbread) arrives fingertip-burning hot and dramatically smeared with za’atar. Everything comes on small plates that do nothing to diminish the dishes’ outsize personalities — and that’s no joke. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Sofreh   

 - Middle Eastern
- $$$
- 75 St. Marks Avenue
- Prospect Heights, Brooklyn
- www.sofrehnyc.com
- Last reviewed on Sept. 11, 2018
- ★★

Jeenah Moon for The New York Times

On a tree-lined street in Prospect Heights, Sofreh fills in a missing piece of New York’s Iranian food scene. The former caterer Nasim Alikhani shows off the glories of spice-scented, orange blossom-sprinkled Persian family cuisine in a welcoming, chic setting. A flattened chicken is served charred at the edges, with a sweet-tart sauce of barberries and apricots; tamarind-soured fish is simmered with so many herbs it could count as a green vegetable. But the jewel in Sofreh’s crown is its perfectly executed, saffron-stained tahdig, with a covetable, golden-crisp layer of rice found at the bottom of the pot. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Superiority Burger   

 - Diner, Vegetarian
- $$
- 119 Avenue A
- East Village, Manhattan
- superiorityburger.com
- Last reviewed on June 27, 2023
- ★★★

Karsten Moran for The New York Times

The chef Brooks Headley’s brain must be a fascinating place. He’s perpetually rewriting the rules of cooking with vegetables, pairing slippery sheets of yuba with charred broccoli in a sandwich, and serving beets tumbled with pretzels and jalapeño cream cheese. And Mr. Headley’s background as a pastry chef shines through in the lush gelato, which comes in flavors like labneh, lychee and cherry leaf. The titular dish — still a standard-bearer for the veggie burger — is just the tip of the iceberg. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

Hannah Wyatt

New York is the kind of town where a person looking to splash out hundreds of dollars on a sushi omakase dinner has a long list of fine options. But those who like their sea creatures pristine and largely unadorned flock to Sushi Noz, where the chef Nozomu Abe graciously presides over an artful parade of seasonal dishes in a hushed yet welcoming room lined with hinoki wood. First come the otsumami, small jewels of appetizers — chunks of octopus with triggerfish, lobes of custardy, saline uni with their deep-sea creaminess, silky slivers of vinegared crab — followed by nigiri so skillfully wrought that they may, for better or worse, have you thinking about taking the plunge again soon. *MELISSA CLARK*

Sushi Ouji

Omakase menus can run up quite a bill in this town ($$$$), and it’s hard to find truly excellent experiences at the other end of the price scale ($). Sushi Ouji brilliantly fills the gap, delivering a carefully curated 14-course selection of inventive otsumami, pristine nigiri and satisfying futomaki, all for a quarter of the price of the more expensive places. Most of the fish is flown in from the Toyosu Market in Tokyo, with the quality and variety consistently superb. The service can feel a little rushed, and maybe the room is too brightly lit, but it’s still one of the best deals in the city. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Taiwanese Gourmet   

 - Taiwanese
- $
- 8402 Broadway
- Elmhurst, Queens

Janice Chung for The New York Times

This cash-only, no-nonsense oasis of Taiwanese cooking has been serving impeccable flies heads (stir-fried flowering chives and ground pork speckled with fermented black beans) and pungent stinky tofu to enthusiastic crowds since the 1990s. All the dishes on the extensive menu are cooked with care and expertise. A whole fish arrives delicately steamed, perfumed with strands of ginger and scallions; bouncy slices of kidney and liver in a concentrated brown glaze are cooked until soft and juicy; braised tofu skin envelops the pork roll, which in turn wraps around bits of daikon and savory minced meat. The move here is to pack the lazy susan on your table by over-ordering, then bring leftovers home to feast on slices of exceptionally crisp fried pork chop all week long. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Temple Canteen   

 - Indian
- $
- 143-09 Holly Avenue
- Flushing, Queens
- canteen.nyganeshtemple.org
- Last reviewed on April 4, 2007

Colin Clark for The New York Times

Beneath the Hindu temple in Flushing, where devotees pray to Lakshmi and Ganesh, you’ll find a cafe serving devotees of dosa, idli and vada. This basement cafeteria specializes in those South Indian stalwarts, offering an impressive variety. The long tables are usually crowded with families polishing off the last bits of coconut chutney or sambhar from stainless steel trays, using their crisp-edged uttapams as napkins. The service is direct and no-nonsense, and so is the food: The rava masala dosa, speckled with chiles and onions and wisped along the edges, is a standout. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

Brittainy Newman/The New York Times

Ann Redding and Matt Danzer have created a particular genre of Thai American cooking that leans hard into fish sauce and chiles and doesn’t take itself too seriously. The retro-looking Thai Diner excels at classic dishes like khao soi and pad Thai, yet also infuses French toast with Thai tea and mixes tom yum soup with tomato bisque. No matter what you order, expect loud, fiery flavors and playful touches, like a pair of googly eyes on your pineapple chiffon cake. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

Justin Sisson

Making good on a lifelong dream to own her own restaurant, Cali Faulkner has created a cozy neighborhood treasure in the heart of Fort Greene. Richly influenced by her time in Northern France and a stint at Verjus in Paris, Ms. Faulkner has devised a concise, seasonal menu, which makes deft use of greenmarket bounty. In spring, that means saucers of morels for snacking (“instead of olives,” as the menu clarifies), a wild-leek tart with buttery crust, pink slices of rhubarb on a duck breast, and — arguably most thrilling — an ebullient, perfectly dressed salad filled with flowers, herbs and a many-textured multitude of vegetables. You can find good duck and morels easily enough in this city, but a salad this excellent is a much rarer bird. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Torrisi   

 - Italian
- $$$$
- 275 Mulberry Street
- NoLIta, Manhattan
- torrisinyc.com
- Last reviewed on Feb. 28, 2023
- ★★★

Evan Sung for The New York Times

A deep love for New York’s culinary history lingers in the food at Torrisi, the stylish reincarnation of the groundbreaking original that put the chef Rich Torrisi and his partners at Major Food Group on the map. Cucumbers New Yorkese, lathered in pickle brine, evoke the city’s best delis, while dishes like cavatelli with a deeply satisfying Jamaican beef ragù are a nod to New York’s many immigrant communities. It’s all presented with the panache that has become this restaurant group’s signature. This is one of New York's great dining rooms, capable of making even a snack at the bar feel like a glamorous night on the town. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

##  Trinciti Roti Shop   

 - Trinidadian and Tobagonian
- $
- 111-03 Lefferts Boulevard
- South Ozone Park, Queens
- trinciti.com

Randy Smith for The New York Times

Here’s a power move for anyone arriving at Kennedy Airport. Take the 15-minute cab ride to Trinciti Roti Shop, order a few doubles, an aloo pie and the curry goat from the charming staff behind the counter. Eat your doubles in the shop, letting the stinging pepper sauce and plump chana dribble down your elbows. Take the rest home to enjoy the next day. Revel in your good fortune at having visited this Trinidadian institution. Welcome back to New York, indeed. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

##  Txikito   

 - Spanish
- $$
- 240 Ninth Avenue
- Chelsea, Manhattan
- txikitonyc.com
- Last reviewed on April 21, 2009
- ★

Nico Schinco for The New York Times

This lively Basque restaurant, which began serving a mix of creative and traditional pintxos in 2008, went on hiatus during the pandemic but reopened with a fresh inventiveness and look in 2023. Small plates issue from Alex Raij and Eder Montero’s tiny kitchen, from familiar tapas to idiosyncratic delights: crisp-skinned suckling pig, briny octopus carpaccio, and boquerones that seem unadorned until you bite into zesty minty leaves of Vietnamese rau ram concealed inside. Txikito’s wide-ranging cooking may originate on the Bay of Biscay, but it doesn’t stay there, driven by a relentless verve and curiosity that couldn’t be more Basque. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Una Pizza Napoletana   

 - Pizza
- $$
- 175 Orchard Street
- Lower East Side, Manhattan
- unapizza.com
- Last reviewed on June 4, 2019
- ★★

Daniel Krieger for The New York Times

As anyone who worships at the altar of Neapolitan-style pizza will attest, the puffy, singed crust and perfectly balanced toppings on Anthony Mangieri’s pies are worthy of devotion. A reservation at Una Pizza Napoletana is a hard get, but Mr. Mangieri always keeps some dough for the walk-ins who line up more than an hour ahead of opening to score one of his tomatoey, olive-oil-slicked disks. There’s not much else on the menu — some marinated olives, a dish of fire-charred peppers, a gelato or two. But the people who show up typically already know their order by heart. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Via Carota   

 - Italian
- $$$$
- 51 Grove Street
- West Village, Manhattan
- viacarota.com
- Last reviewed on March 3, 2015
- ★★

Nico Schinco for The New York Times

Since 2014, Via Carota’s quality has continued to justify the length of the wait for a table. The leafy green salad remains sprightly, the breaded olives encased in pork sausage crisp and brawny, and the pastas supple and amply cheese-dusted. Attention to detail is the through line, from the rustic flea-market appointments to the seasonal Italian cooking and streamlined cocktail list with multiple Negronis. Rabbit is pan-fried to golden perfection, and vegetable dishes like caramelized twigs of salsify or tender poached fennel imbued with orange embody the nonchalant elegance that keep this inviting West Village spot packed from midmorning until late at night. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  Village Café   

 - Azerbaijani
- $$
- 1968 Coney Island Avenue
- Gravesend, Brooklyn
- villagecafeny.com
- Last reviewed on Oct. 2, 2018
- ★★

Randy Smith for The New York Times

Wedged at the back of a small parking lot off Coney Island Avenue, Village Café would be easy to pass right by. But plov lovers know that’s where you go for some of the best Azerbaijani rice pilaf in the city, fragrant with saffron and topped with stewed fruit and gobbets of browned lamb. The soups are equally enticing, particularly the steaming dushbara filled with tiny handmade dumplings, and a magenta borscht bobbing with vegetables and meat. You may be able to find other good Azerbaijani restaurants in New York, but this is the one to save to your Google map. *MELISSA CLARK*

##  White Bear   

 - Chinese
- $
- 135-02 Roosevelt Avenue
- Flushing, Queens

Janice Chung for The New York Times

The pork wontons at this walk-up window in Flushing are a New York treasure: overflowing with pork, stained with a prickly chile oil, doused with scallions and sprinkled with pickled vegetables that punctuate every bite with brine. The rest of the menu is great, too, but it’s the No. 6 — those wontons — that stands apart. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

##  Yoon Haeundae Galbi   

 - Korean
- $$$
- 8 West 36th Street
- Koreatown, Manhattan
- yoon-nyc.com
- Last reviewed on June 1, 2021

Cole Saladino for The New York Times

A grooved, domed surface sits at the center of each table at this Korean barbecue restaurant, and it’s the key, your server will tell you, to producing fatty, cragged edges on the meats, like that of a smash burger. Every cut here is well-marbled and of remarkable quality, but it’s the “Haeundae cut” short rib — slashed repeatedly along the sides to break up the sinew and yield tender, juicy slivers — that shines brightest. *PRIYA KRISHNA*

##  Zaab Zaab   

 - Thai
- $$
- 76-04 Woodside Avenue
- Elmhurst, Queens
- instagram.com/zaabzaabnyc
- Last reviewed on June 28, 2022
- ★★★

Adam Friedlander for The New York Times

Elmhurst’s Zaab Zaab (now with outposts in Brooklyn and Manhattan) stands out for its fiery Isan-style Thai cooking, with a focus on seafood. Come with a group of heat-seekers to explore the menu, whose fiery chiles, dried shrimp and intense fish sauces are used the way an arsonist applies gasoline. The signature dish is arguably the larb ped udon, a punchy mix of duck breast and liver accented with crispy bits of fried duck skin. But if you’re not a liver lover, you might go for the intensely oceanic papaya salad enhanced with house-fermented pla ra. Flexitarians should order both, along with the stellar version of beef kapow, topped with fistfuls of fragrant holy basil. *MELISSA CLARK*
